name: 2 Chronicles
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint (where Chronicles is called Paraleipomena, “things left out”), using Brenton’s public-domain English translation, and against the parallel passages in Genesis, Samuel, Kings, and the Psalms. Only a very small Dead Sea Scrolls fragment of Chronicles survives; it is mentioned only in general terms. Where Chronicles differs from its parallels in names, numbers, or wording, the footnotes say so. Each personal and place name receives a brief note on its meaning at its first mention in Chronicles; many such meanings are uncertain, and the notes say so. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible, which in places differs from the Hebrew; the footnotes give the Hebrew numbering where they differ. Weights and measures are given in modern US units, with the original units and metric figures in the footnotes, and dates are given with their modern-month spans.

verses.text: Solomon the son of David strengthened himself in his kingdom, and Yahweh his God was with him and made him exceedingly great.{a}
Solomon spoke to all Israel, to the commanders of thousands and of hundreds, to the judges, and to every leader in all Israel, the heads of the fathers’ houses.
Then Solomon and all the assembly with him went to the high place at Gibeon, for God’s tent of meeting was there, which Moses the servant of Yahweh had made in the wilderness.{b}
But the ark of God David had brought up from Kiriath-jearim to the place that David had prepared for it, for he had pitched a tent for it in Jerusalem.{c}
And the bronze altar that Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, had made was there before the tabernacle of Yahweh; and Solomon and the assembly sought it.{d}
Solomon went up there to the bronze altar before Yahweh, which was at the tent of meeting, and offered a thousand burnt offerings on it.
In that night God appeared to Solomon and said to him, “Ask what I shall give you.”
Solomon said to God, “You have shown great steadfast love to David my father, and have made me king in his place.
Now, Yahweh God, let your word to David my father be confirmed, for you have made me king over a people as numerous as the dust of the earth.
Give me now wisdom and knowledge, that I may go out and come in before this people; for who can judge this great people of yours?”

God said to Solomon, “Because this was in your heart, and you have not asked for riches, possessions, or honor, nor the life of those who hate you, neither yet have asked for many days, but have asked for yourself wisdom and knowledge so that you may judge my people over whom I have made you king,
wisdom and knowledge are given to you. and I will give you riches, wealth, and honor, such as none of the kings who were before you had, and none after you will have.”
So Solomon came from the high place at Gibeon, from before the tent of meeting, to Jerusalem; and he reigned over Israel.{e}
Solomon gathered chariots and horsemen. He had fourteen hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.{f}
The king made silver and gold in Jerusalem as common as stones, and he made cedars as plentiful as the sycamore-fig trees of the Shephelah.{g}
Solomon’s horses were imported from Egypt and from Kue; the king’s traders bought them from Kue at a price.{h}

They brought up and exported a chariot from Egypt for about fifteen pounds of silver, and a horse for about three and three-quarter pounds; and so they exported them through their hands to all the kings of the Hittites and to the kings of Aram.{i}

notes.text: Verses 1–13 parallel 1 Kings 3:4–15. Solomon, from shalom, “peace.” David, “beloved.”

Gibeon, “hill.” Chronicles explains why Solomon worshiped at Gibeon: the tent of meeting was there (1 Chronicles 16:39; 21:29). Moses, perhaps Egyptian “born,” associated in Exodus 2:10 with Hebrew “drawn out.”
Kiriath-jearim, “city of forests.” Jerusalem, perhaps “foundation of Shalem” or “city of peace.” See 1 Chronicles 13; 15.

Bezalel, “in the shadow of God”; Uri, “my light” or “fiery”; Hur, perhaps “white” or “noble.” The Hebrew vowels read “he had put” (sam) before the tabernacle; the Septuagint reads “was there” (sham), with the same consonants. “Sought it” may mean “sought him,” that is, Yahweh.
Hebrew “to the high place.” The Septuagint reads “from the high place,” as the context requires.
Verses 14–17 parallel 1 Kings 10:26–29; compare 2 Chronicles 9:25–28.
The Shephelah (“lowland”) is the foothill region west of Judah.
Egypt, Hebrew Mitsrayim. Kue is probably Cilicia in southeastern Asia Minor. Some interpreters read “Muzri,” a land in Asia Minor, for “Egypt” in these verses.

Hebrew “six hundred of silver … a hundred and fifty,” probably shekels: about 6.9 kilograms and 1.7 kilograms. Hittites, descendants of Heth; Aram, perhaps “highland,” here the Aramean kingdoms of Syria.

verses.text: Solomon purposed to build a house for the name of Yahweh, and a royal house for himself.{a}
Solomon counted out seventy thousand men to bear burdens, eighty thousand men to quarry stone in the hill country, and three thousand six hundred to oversee them.{b}
Solomon sent to Huram the king of Tyre, saying, “As you dealt with David my father, and sent him cedars to build himself a house to dwell in, so deal with me.{c}

Behold, I am about to build a house for the name of Yahweh my God, to dedicate it to him, to burn before him incense of sweet spices, for the continual showbread, and for burnt offerings morning and evening, on the Sabbaths, on the new moons, and at the appointed feasts of Yahweh our God. This is for Israel forever.
The house that I build is great, for our God is greater than all gods.
But who is able to build him a house, since the heavens, even the highest heavens, cannot contain him? Who am I, then, that I should build him a house, except to burn incense before him?

Now therefore send me a man skillful to work in gold, in silver, in bronze, in iron, and in purple, crimson, and blue, who knows how to engrave engravings, to be with the skilled men who are with me in Judah and Jerusalem, whom David my father provided.{d}
Send me also cedar trees, cypress trees, and algum trees out of Lebanon, for I know that your servants know how to cut timber in Lebanon; and behold, my servants will be with your servants,{e}
even to prepare me timber in plenty; for the house that I am about to build shall be great and wonderful.

Behold, to your servants, the woodcutters who cut the timber, I will give about 120,000 bushels of crushed wheat, about 120,000 bushels of barley, about 120,000 gallons of wine, and about 120,000 gallons of oil.”{f}
Then Huram the king of Tyre answered in a letter that he sent to Solomon: “Because Yahweh loves his people, he has made you king over them.”

Huram also said, “Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, who made the heavens and the earth, who has given King David a wise son, endowed with discretion and understanding, who will build a house for Yahweh and a royal house for himself.
Now I have sent a skilled man, endowed with understanding, Huram-abi,{g}

the son of a woman of the daughters of Dan, whose father was a Tyrian man. He is skillful to work in gold, in silver, in bronze, in iron, in stone, and in timber, in purple, in blue, in fine linen, and in crimson, and to engrave every kind of engraving and to carry out any design that may be given him, together with your skilled men and the skilled men of my lord David your father.{h}
Now therefore the wheat and the barley, the oil and the wine, of which my lord has spoken, let him send to his servants.
And we will cut timber from Lebanon, as much as you need, and bring it to you in rafts by sea to Joppa, and you shall carry it up to Jerusalem.”{i}

Then Solomon counted all the resident foreigners who were in the land of Israel, after the census that David his father had taken of them; and they were found to be a hundred and fifty-three thousand six hundred.{j}
He made seventy thousand of them bearers of burdens, eighty thousand quarriers in the hill country, and three thousand six hundred overseers to make the people work.

notes.text: In Hebrew, 2:1 is 1:18, and 2:2–18 are 2:1–17. Verses 1–18 parallel 1 Kings 5:1–18 (Hebrew 5:15–32).
First Kings 5:16 gives three thousand three hundred overseers. Adding the chief officers (8:10 two hundred fifty; 1 Kings 9:23 five hundred fifty), both books reach a total of 3,850.
Huram, a form of Hiram (as in Kings), perhaps “my brother is exalted.” Tyre, “rock.”
Judah, associated with “praise” (Genesis 29:35).
Lebanon, “white,” from its snow-capped mountains. Algum is an unidentified fine wood; 1 Kings 10:11 has almug.

Hebrew “twenty thousand cors of crushed wheat, twenty thousand cors of barley, twenty thousand baths of wine, and twenty thousand baths of oil.” A cor is about 6 bushels (220 liters), and a bath about 6 gallons (22 liters): about 4,400,000 liters of wheat and of barley, and 440,000 liters each of wine and oil. First Kings 5:11 lists twenty thousand cors of wheat and twenty cors of beaten oil (the Septuagint of Kings, twenty thousand baths).
Huram-abi, “Huram is my father,” or “Huram my master craftsman”; 1 Kings 7:13 calls him Hiram.
First Kings 7:14 says his mother was a widow of the tribe of Naphtali. She may have been of Danite descent living in Naphtali, or the traditions differ. Dan, “judge.”
Joppa, “beautiful,” the port of modern Jaffa.
Compare 1 Chronicles 22:2.

verses.text: Then Solomon began to build the house of Yahweh in Jerusalem on Mount Moriah, where Yahweh had appeared to David his father, at the place that David had prepared, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite.{a}
He began to build on the second day of the second month (in April–May), in the fourth year of his reign.{b}
These are the foundations that Solomon laid for building the house of God: the length, by the old standard of measure, was ninety feet, and the breadth thirty feet.{c}
The porch in front of the house was thirty feet long, matching the breadth of the house, and its height was a hundred and eighty feet; and he overlaid it inside with pure gold.{d}
The great house he paneled with cypress wood, overlaid it with fine gold, and carved palm trees and chains on it.{e}
He adorned the house with precious stones for beauty; and the gold was gold of Parvaim.{f}
He overlaid also the house, the beams, the thresholds, and its walls, and its doors, with gold; and engraved cherubim on the walls.

He made the room of the most holy place. Its length, corresponding to the breadth of the house, was thirty feet, and its breadth thirty feet; and he overlaid it with fine gold amounting to about twenty-two and a half tons.{g}
The weight of the nails was about a pound and a quarter of gold. He overlaid the upper rooms with gold.{h}
In the room of the most holy place he made two cherubim of sculptured work, and they overlaid them with gold.{i}

The wings of the cherubim together were thirty feet long: one wing of the first, seven and a half feet, touched the wall of the house, and its other wing, seven and a half feet, touched the wing of the other cherub.{j}
And one wing of the other cherub, seven and a half feet, touched the wall of the house, and its other wing, seven and a half feet, joined the wing of the first cherub.
The wings of these cherubim spread out thirty feet. They stood on their feet, facing the house.{k}
He made the veil of blue, purple, and crimson yarn and fine linen, and worked cherubim on it.{l}
In front of the house he made two pillars about fifty-two feet high, and the capital on the top of each was seven and a half feet.{m}
He made chains in the inner sanctuary and put them on the tops of the pillars; and he made a hundred pomegranates and put them on the chains.{n}
He set up the pillars in front of the temple, one on the right hand and the other on the left; and called the name of the one on the right hand Jachin, and the name of the one on the left Boaz.{o}

notes.text: Moriah, perhaps “Yahweh provides” or “seen by Yahweh”; only here and in Genesis 22:2 (“the land of Moriah”), linking the temple site with the place of Isaac’s offering. Ornan, see 1 Chronicles 21:15; Jebusite, of Jebus (“trodden place”), the old name of Jerusalem. Verses 1–17 parallel 1 Kings 6–7.

Hebrew “in the second month, on the second”; the second “on the second” is lacking in the Septuagint and may be a copying error. The second month is Ziv (1 Kings 6:1), later Iyyar, counting from the spring new year. First Kings 6:1 dates this to the 480th year after the exodus.

Hebrew “the length in cubits after the first measure was sixty cubits, and the breadth twenty cubits,” about 27 by 9 meters, taking a cubit as 18 inches (45 centimeters). “The first measure” was probably an older, longer cubit of about 20.5 inches (52 centimeters), which would give about 102 by 34 feet. Compare 1 Kings 6:2, which also gives a height of thirty cubits.
Hebrew “twenty cubits … a hundred and twenty,” about 9 and 54 meters. Some Greek manuscripts and the Syriac read “twenty cubits” for the height; 1 Kings 6:3 gives no height for the porch.
“Great house” is the main hall (the holy place).
Parvaim, an unidentified source of gold, perhaps in Arabia.
Hebrew “six hundred talents,” about 20 metric tons, taking a talent as about 75 pounds (34 kilograms). Each dimension here is twenty cubits (about 9 meters).
Hebrew “fifty shekels,” about 575 grams.
The meaning of the Hebrew word for “sculptured work” (tsa‘atsu‘im) is uncertain.
Hebrew “twenty cubits … five cubits”: about 9 meters, and 2.3 meters for each wing. Compare 1 Kings 6:23–28, where the cherubim are of olive wood, ten cubits high.
Or “toward the main hall.”
First Kings does not mention the veil at this point, but describes doors of olive wood (1 Kings 6:31–32).

Hebrew “thirty-five cubits … five cubits,” about 16 meters and 2.3 meters. First Kings 7:15, 2 Kings 25:17, and Jeremiah 52:21 give eighteen cubits (about 27 feet; 8.1 meters) for each pillar; thirty-five may be their combined length, or a different measure. First Kings 7:16 gives the capitals as five cubits; 2 Kings 25:17 gives three.
Hebrew “in the inner sanctuary” (baddevir); many scholars emend to “like a necklace” (karabid), since the chains were on the pillars outside.
Jachin, “he establishes”; Boaz, perhaps “in him is strength.”

verses.text: He made an altar of bronze, thirty feet long, thirty feet broad, and fifteen feet high.{a}
Then he made the Sea of cast metal, fifteen feet from brim to brim, round all about; its height was seven and a half feet, and a line of forty-five feet measured its circumference.{b}
Beneath it, all around, were figures of oxen encircling it, ten to every foot and a half, surrounding the Sea; the oxen were in two rows, cast together with it.{c}

It stood on twelve oxen, three looking toward the north, three toward the west, three toward the south, and three toward the east; and the Sea was set on them above, and all their hind parts were toward the center.
Its thickness was about three inches, and its brim was made like the brim of a cup, like the flower of a lily; it could hold about eighteen thousand gallons.{d}
He also made ten basins for washing, and set five on the right and five on the left. In them they rinsed what was used for the burnt offering, but the Sea was for the priests to wash in.
He made the ten lampstands of gold as prescribed for them, and set them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left.{e}
He made ten tables and placed them in the temple, five on the right and five on the left; and he made a hundred basins of gold.{f}
He made the court of the priests and the great court, and doors for the court, and overlaid their doors with bronze.
He set the Sea at the right side of the house, to the southeast.
Huram also made the pots, the shovels, and the basins. So Huram completed the work that he did for King Solomon on the house of God:{g}
the two pillars, and the bowls and the two capitals on the tops of the pillars, and the two networks to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the tops of the pillars;
and the four hundred pomegranates for the two networks, two rows of pomegranates for each network, to cover the two bowls of the capitals that were on the pillars.
He made the stands, and the basins on the stands;{h}
the one Sea, and the twelve oxen under it.
The pots, the shovels, the forks, and all their utensils Huram-abi made of burnished bronze for King Solomon for the house of Yahweh.{i}
In the plain of the Jordan the king cast them, in the clay ground between Succoth and Zeredah.{j}
Solomon made all these utensils in very great quantity, for the weight of the bronze was not sought out.
So Solomon made all the vessels that were in the house of God: the golden altar, the tables with the bread of the Presence on them,{k}
and the lampstands with their lamps of pure gold, to burn according to the ordinance in front of the inner sanctuary;
the flowers, the lamps, and the tongs, of gold, of the most perfect gold;

the snuffers, the basins, the dishes for incense, and the fire pans, of pure gold; and as for the entrance of the house, its inner doors to the most holy place and the doors of the house, the main hall, were of gold.{l}

notes.text: Hebrew “twenty cubits long, twenty cubits broad, and ten cubits high,” about 9 by 9 by 4.5 meters. This altar is not described in the standard text of 1 Kings 7, though 1 Kings 8:64 and 9:25 mention it. Verses 2–5 parallel 1 Kings 7:23–26.
Hebrew “ten cubits … five cubits … thirty cubits”: about 4.5 meters across, 2.3 meters high, and 13.5 meters around. The round figure thirty for the circumference is an approximation.
Hebrew “ten in a cubit.” First Kings 7:24 has “gourds” (peqa‘im) instead of “oxen” (beqarim); the two Hebrew words look alike.

Hebrew “a handbreadth” (about 7.5 centimeters) and “three thousand baths” (about 66,000 liters). First Kings 7:26 gives two thousand baths (about 12,000 gallons; 44,000 liters). Chronicles may include the capacity to the brim, or the figures reflect different measures.
Compare Exodus 25:31–40; 1 Kings 7:49 also has ten lampstands.
Or “bowls” for sprinkling.
Huram, see 2:3. Verses 11–22 parallel 1 Kings 7:40–50. Hebrew “Huram” here and “Huram-abi” in verse 16; Kings has Hiram.
Hebrew “he made the stands, and he made the basins”; compare 1 Kings 7:43.
Hebrew “Huram his father”; see 2:13.
Jordan, “descender.” Succoth, “booths.” Zeredah (1 Kings 7:46 Zarethan), perhaps “cooling.”
Hebrew “bread of the face”; see 1 Chronicles 9:32.
Or “the hinges of the doors”; compare 1 Kings 7:50.

verses.text: Thus all the work that Solomon did for the house of Yahweh was finished. And Solomon brought in the holy things of David his father, the silver, the gold, and all the vessels, and put them in the treasuries of the house of God.{a}

Then Solomon assembled the elders of Israel and all the heads of the tribes, the leaders of the fathers’ houses of the people of Israel, to Jerusalem, to bring up the ark of the covenant of Yahweh out of the city of David, which is Zion.{b}
And all the men of Israel assembled before the king at the feast in the seventh month (in September–October).{c}
All the elders of Israel came, and the Levites took up the ark.{d}
They brought up the ark, the tent of meeting, and all the holy vessels that were in the tent; the priests, the Levites, brought them up.{e}
King Solomon and all the congregation of Israel who had gathered to him were before the ark, sacrificing sheep and oxen so many that they could not be counted or numbered.
Then the priests brought the ark of the covenant of Yahweh to its place, into the inner sanctuary of the house, the most holy place, beneath the wings of the cherubim.
For the cherubim spread out their wings over the place of the ark, and the cherubim covered the ark and its poles from above.
The poles were so long that the ends of the poles were seen from the ark in front of the inner sanctuary, but they could not be seen from outside; and it is there to this day.{f}
There was nothing in the ark except the two tablets that Moses put there at Horeb, where Yahweh made a covenant with the people of Israel when they came out of Egypt.{g}
Now when the priests came out of the holy place (for all the priests who were present had consecrated themselves, without keeping to their divisions,{h}

and the Levitical singers, all of them, Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun, with their sons and brothers, arrayed in fine linen, having cymbals and stringed instruments and harps, stood at the east end of the altar, and with them a hundred and twenty priests blowing trumpets),{i}

it came to pass, when the trumpeters and the singers were as one, to make one sound heard in praising and thanking Yahweh, and when they raised the sound with trumpets and cymbals and instruments of song, and praised Yahweh, “For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever,” that the house, the house of Yahweh, was filled with a cloud,{j}
so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of Yahweh filled the house of God.

notes.text: Verses 1–14 parallel 1 Kings 7:51–8:11.
Zion, perhaps “fortress” or “dry place.”
Hebrew “at the feast; it was the seventh month,” the month Ethanim (1 Kings 8:2), later Tishri, counting from the spring new year. The feast is Booths (compare 7:8–10).
First Kings 8:3 reads “the priests took up the ark.” Chronicles names the Levites, in keeping with 1 Chronicles 15:2.
The Septuagint and 1 Kings 8:4 read “the priests and the Levites.”
Hebrew “it is there”; the Septuagint and 1 Kings 8:8 read “they are there.”
Horeb, “dry” or “desolate,” another name for Mount Sinai.
Verses 11b–13a are not in 1 Kings 8:10–11. Compare 1 Chronicles 24.
Asaph, “he gathers”; Heman, “faithful”; Jeduthun, perhaps “praising.” See 1 Chronicles 25.
This refrain appears also at 7:3, 6; 20:21; compare 1 Chronicles 16:34; Psalm 136.

verses.text: Then Solomon said, “Yahweh has said that he would dwell in thick darkness.{a}
But I have built you a lofty house, an established place for your dwelling forever.”{b}
Then the king turned his face and blessed all the assembly of Israel, while all the assembly of Israel stood.
And he said, “Blessed be Yahweh, the God of Israel, who spoke with his mouth to David my father, and with his hands has fulfilled it, saying,

‘Since the day that I brought my people out of the land of Egypt, I chose no city among all the tribes of Israel to build a house in, that my name might be there; neither did I choose any man to be leader over my people Israel;{c}
but I have chosen Jerusalem, that my name might be there, and I have chosen David to be over my people Israel.’
Now it was in the heart of David my father to build a house for the name of Yahweh, the God of Israel.
But Yahweh said to David my father, ‘Since it was in your heart to build a house for my name, you did well that it was in your heart.
Nevertheless, you shall not build the house; but your son who will come forth from your loins, he shall build the house for my name.’

Now Yahweh has established his word that he spoke; for I have risen in the place of David my father and sit on the throne of Israel, as Yahweh promised, and I have built the house for the name of Yahweh, the God of Israel.
And there I have set the ark, in which is the covenant of Yahweh that he made with the people of Israel.”
Then he stood before the altar of Yahweh in the presence of all the assembly of Israel and spread out his hands.

For Solomon had made a bronze platform seven and a half feet long, seven and a half feet broad, and four and a half feet high, and had set it in the middle of the court; and he stood on it. Then he knelt on his knees before all the assembly of Israel and spread out his hands toward heaven,{d}
and said, “Yahweh, God of Israel, there is no God like you in the heavens or in the earth, who keeps covenant and lovingkindness with your servants who walk before you with all their heart;
who have kept with your servant David my father what you promised him. You spoke with your mouth, and with your hand you have fulfilled it, as at this day.

Now therefore, Yahweh, God of Israel, keep for your servant David my father what you promised him, saying, ‘There shall not fail you a man before me to sit on the throne of Israel, if only your sons keep their way, to walk in my law as you have walked before me.’{e}
Now therefore, Yahweh, God of Israel, let your word be confirmed, which you spoke to your servant David.
“But will God indeed dwell with man on the earth? Behold, the heavens and the highest heavens cannot contain you, how much less this house that I have built!{f}
Yet turn to the prayer of your servant and to his plea, Yahweh my God, to listen to the cry and to the prayer that your servant prays before you,
that your eyes may be open toward this house day and night, toward the place where you have said you would put your name, to listen to the prayer that your servant prays toward this place.
And listen to the pleas of your servant and of your people Israel, which they pray toward this place; hear from the place of your dwelling, from heaven; and when you hear, forgive.
“If a man sins against his neighbor, and an oath is laid on him to make him swear, and he comes and swears before your altar in this house,{g}
then hear from heaven, and act, and judge your servants, requiting the wicked, to bring his way upon his own head, and justifying the righteous, to give him according to his righteousness.
“If your people Israel are defeated before an enemy because they have sinned against you, and they turn back and confess your name and pray and plead before you in this house,
then hear from heaven and forgive the sin of your people Israel, and bring them back to the land that you gave to them and to their fathers.
“When the heavens are shut up and there is no rain because they have sinned against you, if they pray toward this place and confess your name and turn from their sin, because you afflict them,

then hear in heaven and forgive the sin of your servants, your people Israel, when you teach them the good way in which they should walk, and give rain on your land, which you have given to your people as an inheritance.

“If there is famine in the land, if there is pestilence, blight, or mildew, locust or grasshopper; if their enemies besiege them in the land of their gates; whatever plague, whatever sickness there is,{h}
whatever prayer, whatever plea is made by any man or by all your people Israel, who shall know every man his own plague and his own sorrow, and shall spread out his hands toward this house,
then hear from heaven, your dwelling place, and forgive, and render to each according to all his ways, whose heart you know (for you, you alone, know the hearts of the children of mankind),
that they may fear you, to walk in your ways all the days that they live on the face of the land that you gave to our fathers.

“Also concerning the foreigner, who is not of your people Israel, when he comes from a far country for your great name’s sake, and your mighty hand, and your outstretched arm; when they come and pray toward this house,

hear from heaven, from your dwelling place, and do according to all for which the foreigner calls to you, so that all the peoples of the earth may know your name and fear you, as do your people Israel, and may know that this house that I have built is called by your name.
“If your people go out to battle against their enemies, by whatever way you send them, and they pray to you toward this city that you have chosen and the house that I have built for your name,
then hear from heaven their prayer and their supplication, and maintain their cause.
“If they sin against you (for there is no man who does not sin), and you are angry with them and give them to an enemy, and their captors carry them away captive to a land far or near,

yet if they come to their senses in the land where they are carried captive, and turn again and make supplication to you in the land of their captivity, saying, ‘We have sinned, we have done wrong, we have acted wickedly,’

if they return to you with all their heart and with all their soul in the land of their captivity, where they have been carried captive, and pray toward their land which you gave to their fathers, and the city that you have chosen, and the house that I have built for your name,
then hear from heaven, from your dwelling place, their prayer and their pleas, and maintain their cause, and forgive your people who have sinned against you.
Now, my God, let, I beg you, your eyes be open, and let your ears be attentive to the prayer that is made in this place.{i}
“And now arise, Yahweh God, to your resting place, you and the ark of your might. Let your priests, Yahweh God, be clothed with salvation, and let your faithful ones rejoice in what is good.{j}
Yahweh God, do not turn away the face of your anointed one. Remember the steadfast love for David your servant.”{k}

notes.text: Verses 1–39 parallel 1 Kings 8:12–50.
Hebrew zevul, “exalted dwelling” or “princely house.”
First Kings 8:16 lacks the words “and I chose no man … but I have chosen Jerusalem, that my name might be there,” though the Septuagint of Kings has a similar clause about choosing Jerusalem.
Hebrew “five cubits long, five cubits broad, and three cubits high,” about 2.3 by 2.3 by 1.4 meters. This verse is not in 1 Kings 8.
First Kings 8:25 reads “to walk before me.” Chronicles stresses the law.
Or “the heavens and the heavens of heavens.” Chronicles adds “with man” (compare 1 Kings 8:27).
Hebrew “and he lays an oath on him to cause him to swear.”
Or “in any of their cities.” Hebrew “in the land of their gates.”
Verses 40–42 differ from the ending of Solomon’s prayer in 1 Kings 8:50–53. Verses 41–42 are drawn from Psalm 132:8–10, 1.
Hebrew hasidim, “those who are faithful” or “godly ones.”
Or “Remember the deeds of steadfast love of David your servant.” Compare Isaiah 55:3; Psalm 132:1.

verses.text: When Solomon had finished praying, fire came down from heaven and consumed the burnt offering and the sacrifices, and the glory of Yahweh filled the house.{a}
The priests could not enter the house of Yahweh, because the glory of Yahweh had filled the house of Yahweh.

All the children of Israel looked on as the fire came down and the glory of Yahweh was on the house, and they bowed with their faces to the earth on the pavement, and worshiped and gave thanks to Yahweh, saying, “For he is good, for his steadfast love endures forever.”
Then the king and all the people offered sacrifice before Yahweh.{b}
King Solomon offered a sacrifice of twenty-two thousand oxen and a hundred and twenty thousand sheep. So the king and all the people dedicated the house of God.

The priests stood at their posts, and the Levites with the instruments for the music of Yahweh that King David had made for giving thanks to Yahweh, “for his steadfast love endures forever,” whenever David offered praise by their hand; and the priests opposite them blew trumpets, and all Israel stood.

And Solomon consecrated the middle of the court that was before the house of Yahweh, for there he offered the burnt offerings and the fat of the peace offerings, because the bronze altar that Solomon had made was not able to receive the burnt offering, the grain offering, and the fat.
So Solomon kept the feast at that time seven days, and all Israel with him, a very great congregation, from the entrance of Hamath to the Brook of Egypt.{c}
On the eighth day they held a solemn assembly, for they had kept the dedication of the altar seven days and the feast seven days.{d}

On the twenty-third day of the seventh month (in September–October) he sent the people away to their tents, rejoicing and glad of heart for the good that Yahweh had done for David and for Solomon and for Israel his people.{e}
Thus Solomon finished the house of Yahweh and the king’s house. And all that came into Solomon’s heart to make in the house of Yahweh and in his own house, he prosperously carried out.{f}
Then Yahweh appeared to Solomon in the night and said to him, “I have heard your prayer and have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice.
When I shut up the heavens so that there is no rain, or command the locust to devour the land, or send pestilence among my people,{g}
and my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven and will forgive their sin and heal their land.
Now my eyes will be open and my ears attentive to the prayer of this place.
For now I have chosen and sanctified this house, that my name may be there forever; and my eyes and my heart shall be there perpetually.
And as for you, if you walk before me as David your father walked, doing according to all that I have commanded you and keeping my statutes and my ordinances,
then I will establish the throne of your kingdom, as I covenanted with David your father, saying, ‘There shall not fail you a man to rule in Israel.’{h}
But if you turn aside and forsake my statutes and my commandments that I have set before you, and go and serve other gods and bow down to them,{i}

then I will uproot them from my land that I have given them, and this house that I have consecrated for my name I will cast out of my sight, and I will make it a proverb and a byword among all peoples.
And this house, which was exalted, everyone passing by it will be appalled and will say, ‘Why has Yahweh done thus to this land and to this house?’{j}

Then they will say, ‘Because they forsook Yahweh, the God of their fathers, who brought them out of the land of Egypt, and laid hold on other gods and bowed down to them and served them; therefore he has brought all this evil upon them.’”

notes.text: Fire from heaven is not mentioned in 1 Kings 8:54; compare 1 Chronicles 21:26; Leviticus 9:24.
Verses 4–10 parallel 1 Kings 8:62–66.
Lebo-hamath, “entrance of Hamath,” the northern limit of the land; Hamath, “fortress.” The Brook of Egypt is probably the Wadi el-Arish, the southern limit.
The feast is Booths, which began on the fifteenth of the seventh month (Leviticus 23:34–36); the dedication of the altar was held the week before.

The seventh month is Ethanim (1 Kings 8:2), later Tishri, counting from the spring new year. First Kings 8:66 says “on the eighth day he sent the people away”; Chronicles counts the final assembly before their departure the next day.
Verses 11–22 parallel 1 Kings 9:1–9.
Verses 13–15 are not in 1 Kings 9.
First Kings 9:5 reads “a man on the throne of Israel.” Compare Micah 5:2.
“You” here is plural, addressing Solomon and the people.
Hebrew “which was high.” Some propose reading “will become a heap of ruins” (compare 1 Kings 9:8).

verses.text: At the end of twenty years, in which Solomon had built the house of Yahweh and his own house,{a}
Solomon built the cities that Huram had given to Solomon, and caused the children of Israel to dwell there.{b}
Solomon went to Hamath-zobah and took it by force.{c}
He built Tadmor in the wilderness and all the store cities that he built in Hamath.{d}
He also built Beth-horon the upper and Beth-horon the lower, fortified cities, with walls, gates, and bars,{e}

and Baalath, and all the store cities that Solomon had, and all the cities for his chariots and the cities for his horsemen, and whatever Solomon desired to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and in all the land of his rule.{f}
All the people who were left of the Hittites, the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, who were not of Israel,{g}
from their descendants who were left after them in the land, whom the people of Israel had not destroyed, Solomon raised a forced labor force, as it is to this day.
But of the people of Israel Solomon made no slaves for his work; they were men of war, and commanders of his officers, and commanders of his chariots and his horsemen.
These were the chief officers of King Solomon, two hundred and fifty, who ruled over the people.{h}

Solomon brought Pharaoh’s daughter up from the city of David to the house he had built for her, for he said, “My wife shall not dwell in the house of David king of Israel, for the places to which the ark of Yahweh has come are holy.”{i}
Then Solomon offered burnt offerings to Yahweh on the altar of Yahweh that he had built before the porch,

even as the duty of every day required, offering according to the commandment of Moses on the Sabbaths, on the new moons, and the appointed feasts three times a year: the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Booths.{j}

According to the ordinance of David his father, he appointed the divisions of the priests for their service, and the Levites for their duties of praise and of ministering before the priests as the duty of each day required, and the gatekeepers in their divisions for each gate; for so David the man of God had commanded.
And they did not turn aside from the king’s command to the priests and Levites concerning any matter, or concerning the treasuries.
So all the work of Solomon was carried out from the day the foundation of the house of Yahweh was laid until it was finished. The house of Yahweh was complete.{k}
Then Solomon went to Ezion-geber and to Eloth on the seashore in the land of Edom.{l}

And Huram sent him, by the hand of his servants, ships and servants who knew the sea; and they went with the servants of Solomon to Ophir, and took from there about seventeen tons of gold and brought it to King Solomon.{m}

notes.text: Verses 1–18 parallel 1 Kings 9:10–28.
First Kings 9:10–14 says Solomon gave Hiram twenty cities in Galilee, which displeased him. Chronicles may describe their return, or follows a different tradition.
Hamath-zobah, Hamath in the region of Zobah (“station”). No campaign of Solomon is recorded in Kings.
Tadmor, “palm,” later Palmyra in the Syrian desert. First Kings 9:18 has Tamar (Ketiv), a town in the southern wilderness of Judah, with Qere Tadmor.
Beth-horon, “house of the hollow.”
Baalath, “lady,” a town of Dan (Joshua 19:44).
Hittites, see 1:17; Amorites, “westerners” or “mountain dwellers”; Perizzites, “villagers”; Hivites, perhaps “tent villagers”; Jebusites, see 3:1.
First Kings 9:23 gives five hundred fifty. See 2:2 note.
Pharaoh, Egyptian “great house,” the title of Egypt’s king. The reason given here is not in 1 Kings 9:24.
Compare Exodus 23:14–17; Deuteronomy 16:16. Booths, Hebrew Sukkot.
Hebrew “until its finishing”; the Septuagint reads “until Solomon finished the house of the Lord.”
Ezion-geber, perhaps “backbone of a strong man”; Eloth (Elath), “terebinths”; Edom, “red.”

Hebrew “four hundred and fifty talents,” about 15.3 metric tons. First Kings 9:28 gives four hundred twenty talents. Kings says Solomon built a fleet and Hiram sent sailors (9:26–27). Ophir, see 1 Chronicles 29:4.

verses.text: When the queen of Sheba heard of the fame of Solomon, she came to Jerusalem to test Solomon with riddles, with a very great retinue and camels bearing spices and very much gold and precious stones. When she came to Solomon, she spoke with him of all that was in her heart.{a}
Solomon told her all her questions, and there was nothing hid from Solomon which he did not tell her.
When the queen of Sheba saw the wisdom of Solomon, the house that he had built,

the food of his table, the seating of his officials, the standing of his ministers and their apparel, his cupbearers and their apparel, and his ascent by which he went up to the house of Yahweh, there was no more breath in her.{b}
And she said to the king, “True was the report that I heard in my own land of your words and of your wisdom.
But I did not believe their words until I came and my own eyes had seen it. And behold, not half of the greatness of your wisdom was told to me; you surpass the report that I heard.
Blessed are your men, and blessed are these your servants who stand continually before you and hear your wisdom!{c}

Blessed be Yahweh your God, who delighted in you to set you on his throne as king for Yahweh your God! Because your God loved Israel, to establish them forever, he has made you king over them, to execute justice and righteousness.”{d}
She gave the king about four and a half tons of gold, and spices in great abundance, and precious stones; neither was there ever such spices as those the queen of Sheba gave to King Solomon.{e}
Moreover the servants of Huram and the servants of Solomon, who brought gold from Ophir, brought algum wood and precious stones.
And the king made from the algum wood steps for the house of Yahweh and for the king’s house, and lyres and harps for the singers; none like them had been seen before in the land of Judah.{f}
King Solomon gave the queen of Sheba all she desired, whatever she asked, besides what she had brought to the king. Then she turned and went to her own land, she and her servants.{g}
The weight of gold that came to Solomon in one year was about twenty-five tons of gold,{h}
besides what the traders and merchants brought. And all the kings of Arabia and the governors of the land brought gold and silver to Solomon.{i}
King Solomon made two hundred large shields of beaten gold; about fifteen pounds of beaten gold went into each large shield.{j}
And he made three hundred small shields of beaten gold; about seven and a half pounds of gold went into each shield. The king put them in the House of the Forest of Lebanon.{k}
The king also made a great throne of ivory and overlaid it with pure gold.
There were six steps to the throne, with a footstool of gold, which were fastened to the throne, and stays on either side by the place of the seat, and two lions standing beside the stays;{l}
and twelve lions stood there on the one side and on the other upon the six steps; there was not the like made in any kingdom.
All King Solomon’s drinking vessels were of gold, and all the vessels of the House of the Forest of Lebanon were of pure gold; silver was not counted as anything in the days of Solomon.
For the king’s ships went to Tarshish with the servants of Huram; once every three years the ships of Tarshish came, bringing gold, silver, ivory, apes, and peacocks.{m}
Thus King Solomon excelled all the kings of the earth in riches and in wisdom.
And all the kings of the earth sought the presence of Solomon to hear his wisdom, which God had put in his heart.
They brought every man his tribute: vessels of silver and vessels of gold, clothing, weapons, spices, horses, and mules, so much year by year.{n}
Solomon had four thousand stalls for horses and chariots, and twelve thousand horsemen, whom he stationed in the chariot cities and with the king in Jerusalem.{o}
He ruled over all the kings from the River to the land of the Philistines and to the border of Egypt.{p}
The king made silver as common in Jerusalem as stones, and he made cedars as plentiful as the sycamore-fig trees of the Shephelah.
And horses were brought for Solomon from Egypt and from all lands.

Now the rest of the acts of Solomon, first and last, are they not written in the words of Nathan the prophet, and in the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and in the visions of Iddo the seer concerning Jeroboam the son of Nebat?{q}
Solomon reigned in Jerusalem over all Israel forty years.
And Solomon slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David his father; and Rehoboam his son reigned in his place.{r}

notes.text: Verses 1–12 parallel 1 Kings 10:1–13. Sheba, probably in southwest Arabia (modern Yemen).
Or “his burnt offerings that he offered at the house of Yahweh”; 1 Kings 10:5 has “his burnt offering.” The Hebrew here, ‘aliyyato, means “his ascent” or “his upper chamber.”
The Septuagint of Kings reads “your wives” for “your men” in 1 Kings 10:8; the Hebrew words are similar.
First Kings 10:9 reads “on the throne of Israel”; Chronicles speaks of the throne as God’s own.
Hebrew “a hundred and twenty talents,” about 4.1 metric tons.
Or “paths” or “stairs”; the Hebrew (mesillot) is uncertain. First Kings 10:12 has “supports” or “railings” (mis‘ad).
The Hebrew text is difficult; it may mean “besides what she had brought in exchange.”
Verses 13–28 parallel 1 Kings 10:14–29. Hebrew “six hundred and sixty-six talents,” about 22.6 metric tons.
Arabia, “steppe” or “desert.”
Hebrew “six hundred of beaten gold,” probably shekels: about 6.9 kilograms.

Hebrew “three hundred of gold,” probably shekels: about 3.45 kilograms. First Kings 10:17 has “three minas of gold,” about 1.7 kilograms if a mina is fifty shekels. On the House of the Forest of Lebanon see 1 Kings 7:2–5.
First Kings 10:19 describes a rounded top to the throne instead of the footstool. The Hebrew words are not alike.

First Kings 10:22 reads “the king had a fleet of ships of Tarshish,” probably large seagoing ships; Chronicles has the ships go to Tarshish (perhaps Tartessus in Spain). “Peacocks” may be baboons; the meaning of the Hebrew (tukkiyyim) is uncertain.
Or “myrrh” for “weapons”; the Hebrew (nesheq) is uncertain.
First Kings 4:26 (Hebrew 5:6) gives forty thousand stalls; many think four thousand original. Compare 1:14; 1 Kings 10:26.
The River is the Euphrates. Philistines, perhaps “wanderers” or “immigrants.”

Compare 1 Kings 11:41, which cites “the book of the acts of Solomon.” Nathan, “he has given”; Ahijah, “brother of Yahweh”; Shilonite, of Shiloh; Iddo, perhaps “timely” or “adorned”; Jeroboam, perhaps “the people contends” or “may the people increase”; Nebat, “he has looked.” Chronicles omits the account of Solomon’s wives and the revolts of 1 Kings 11.
Rehoboam, “the people is enlarged.”

verses.text: Rehoboam went to Shechem, for all Israel had come to Shechem to make him king.{a}
And when Jeroboam the son of Nebat heard of it (for he was in Egypt, where he had fled from King Solomon), Jeroboam returned from Egypt.{b}
They sent and called him, and Jeroboam and all Israel came and spoke to Rehoboam, saying,
“Your father made our yoke hard. Now therefore lighten the hard service of your father and his heavy yoke that he put on us, and we will serve you.”
He said to them, “Return to me after three days.” So the people went away.
Then King Rehoboam consulted with the old men who had stood before Solomon his father while he was alive, saying, “How do you advise me to answer this people?”
They spoke to him, saying, “If you will be good to this people and please them and speak good words to them, they will be your servants all the days.”
But he forsook the counsel that the old men gave him, and consulted with the young men who had grown up with him and stood before him.
He said to them, “What counsel do you give, that we may return answer to this people, who have spoken to me, saying, ‘Make the yoke that your father put on us lighter’?”

The young men who had grown up with him spoke to him, saying, “Thus you shall tell the people who spoke to you, saying, ‘Your father made our yoke heavy, but make it lighter for us’; thus you shall say to them, ‘My little finger is thicker than my father’s loins.{c}
And now, whereas my father laid on you a heavy yoke, I will add to your yoke. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions.’”{d}
So Jeroboam and all the people came to Rehoboam on the third day, as the king had said, “Return to me on the third day.”
And the king answered them harshly; King Rehoboam forsook the counsel of the old men,

and spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men, saying, “My father made your yoke heavy, but I will add to it. My father disciplined you with whips, but I will discipline you with scorpions.”
So the king did not listen to the people, for it was brought about by God, that Yahweh might establish his word, which he spoke by Ahijah the Shilonite to Jeroboam the son of Nebat.{e}

When all Israel saw that the king did not listen to them, the people answered the king, saying, “What portion have we in David? We have no inheritance in the son of Jesse. To your tents, each man, O Israel! Now see to your own house, David.” So all Israel went to their tents.{f}
But as for the people of Israel who lived in the cities of Judah, Rehoboam reigned over them.

Then King Rehoboam sent Hadoram, who was over the forced labor, and the people of Israel stoned him with stones, and he died. And King Rehoboam made haste to mount his chariot to flee to Jerusalem.{g}
So Israel rebelled against the house of David to this day.

notes.text: Verses 1–19 parallel 1 Kings 12:1–19. Rehoboam, see 9:31. Shechem, “shoulder” or “ridge.”

First Kings 12:2 reads “Jeroboam stayed in Egypt”; the Hebrew words for “returned” and “stayed” are similar (wayyashov, wayyeshev). Chronicles assumes the account of Jeroboam in 1 Kings 11:26–40, which it does not include.
Hebrew “than my father’s loins,” that is, his waist.
“Scorpions” may be whips tipped with barbs or metal points.
Ahijah, see 9:29; compare 1 Kings 11:29–39.
Jesse, perhaps “Yahweh exists” or “gift.”
Hadoram, perhaps “Hadad is exalted”; 1 Kings 12:18 has Adoram, and 1 Kings 4:6 Adoniram.

verses.text: When Rehoboam came to Jerusalem, he assembled the house of Judah and Benjamin, a hundred and eighty thousand chosen warriors, to fight against Israel, to restore the kingdom to Rehoboam.{a}
But the word of Yahweh came to Shemaiah the man of God, saying,{b}
“Say to Rehoboam the son of Solomon, king of Judah, and to all Israel in Judah and Benjamin,

‘Thus says Yahweh: You shall not go up or fight against your brothers. Return every man to his house, for this thing is from me.’” So they listened to the words of Yahweh and turned back from going against Jeroboam.
Rehoboam dwelt in Jerusalem, and built cities for defense in Judah.{c}
He built Bethlehem, Etam, Tekoa,{d}
Beth-zur, Soco, Adullam,{e}
Gath, Mareshah, Ziph,{f}
Adoraim, Lachish, Azekah,{g}
Zorah, Aijalon, and Hebron, which are fortified cities in Judah and in Benjamin.{h}
He fortified the strongholds and put captains in them, with stores of food, oil, and wine.
And in every city he put shields and spears and made them very strong. So he held Judah and Benjamin.
And the priests and the Levites who were in all Israel presented themselves to him from all their territory.
For the Levites left their pasture lands and their possession and came to Judah and Jerusalem; for Jeroboam and his sons cast them off, that they should not execute the priest’s office to Yahweh;
and he appointed for himself priests for the high places, and for the goat idols, and for the calves which he had made.{i}
And after them, out of all the tribes of Israel, those who had set their hearts to seek Yahweh, the God of Israel, came to Jerusalem to sacrifice to Yahweh, the God of their fathers.
They strengthened the kingdom of Judah and made Rehoboam the son of Solomon secure for three years, for they walked for three years in the way of David and Solomon.
Rehoboam took as wife Mahalath the daughter of Jerimoth the son of David, and of Abihail the daughter of Eliab the son of Jesse.{j}
She bore him sons: Jeush, Shemariah, and Zaham.{k}
After her he took Maacah the daughter of Absalom, and she bore him Abijah, Attai, Ziza, and Shelomith.{l}
Rehoboam loved Maacah the daughter of Absalom above all his wives and his concubines (for he took eighteen wives and sixty concubines, and fathered twenty-eight sons and sixty daughters).
And Rehoboam appointed Abijah the son of Maacah as chief, as leader among his brothers, for he intended to make him king.
He dealt wisely, and dispersed of all his sons throughout all the lands of Judah and Benjamin, to every fortified city; and he gave them food in abundance, and he sought for them many wives.{m}

notes.text: Verses 1–4 parallel 1 Kings 12:21–24. Benjamin, “son of the right hand” or “son of the south.”
Shemaiah, “Yahweh has heard.”
Verses 5–23 have no parallel in Kings.
Bethlehem, “house of bread”; Etam, perhaps “place of birds of prey”; Tekoa, perhaps “trumpet blast.”
Beth-zur, “house of rock”; Soco, perhaps “thorny” or “branches”; Adullam, perhaps “refuge.”
Gath, “winepress”; Mareshah, “summit”; Ziph, perhaps “refining” or “flowing.”
Adoraim, perhaps “two mounds”; Lachish, meaning uncertain; Azekah, perhaps “hoed ground.”
Zorah, perhaps “hornet”; Aijalon, “place of deer”; Hebron, “association” or “alliance.”
Hebrew se‘irim, “goats” or “hairy ones,” goat-shaped demons; compare Leviticus 17:7. On the calves see 1 Kings 12:28–33.

The Ketiv reads “son of Jerimoth”; the Qere, “daughter of Jerimoth.” Mahalath, perhaps “sickness” or “lyre” (compare the Psalm titles); Jerimoth, “heights”; Abihail, “my father is strength”; Eliab, “my God is father.” Jerimoth is not among David’s sons in 1 Chronicles 3.
Jeush, “he comes to help”; Shemariah, “Yahweh keeps”; Zaham, perhaps “loathing.”

Hebrew “daughter” may mean “granddaughter”; 13:2 calls Abijah’s mother Micaiah the daughter of Uriel. Maacah, perhaps “oppression” or “dull”; Absalom, “father of peace” (1 Kings 15:2 Abishalom); Abijah, “Yahweh is my father” (1 Kings 15:1 Abijam); Attai, perhaps “timely”; Ziza, “abundance”; Shelomith, “peaceful.”
Hebrew “and he asked for a multitude of wives.”

verses.text: When the kingdom of Rehoboam was established and he was strong, he forsook the law of Yahweh, and all Israel with him.{a}
In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, because they had been unfaithful to Yahweh, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem{b}
with twelve hundred chariots and sixty thousand horsemen. And the people who came with him from Egypt were without number: Libyans, Sukkiim, and Cushites.{c}
He took the fortified cities which belonged to Judah, and came to Jerusalem.

Then Shemaiah the prophet came to Rehoboam and to the princes of Judah who had gathered at Jerusalem because of Shishak, and said to them, “Thus says Yahweh: You forsook me, so I also have forsaken you into the hand of Shishak.”
Then the princes of Israel and the king humbled themselves and said, “Yahweh is righteous.”

When Yahweh saw that they humbled themselves, the word of Yahweh came to Shemaiah, saying, “They have humbled themselves; I will not destroy them, but I will grant them deliverance in a little while, and my wrath shall not be poured out on Jerusalem by the hand of Shishak.{d}
Nevertheless they shall be his servants, so that they may know my service and the service of the kingdoms of the lands.”

So Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem. He took away the treasures of the house of Yahweh and the treasures of the king’s house; he took everything. He also took away the shields of gold that Solomon had made,{e}
King Rehoboam made shields of bronze in their place, and committed them to the hands of the captains of the runners, who kept the door of the king’s house.{f}
And whenever the king went into the house of Yahweh, the runners came and carried them and brought them back to the guardroom of the runners.
And when he humbled himself, the wrath of Yahweh turned from him, so as not to destroy him completely. Moreover, conditions were good in Judah.{g}

So King Rehoboam strengthened himself in Jerusalem and reigned. Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he began to reign, and he reigned seventeen years in Jerusalem, the city that Yahweh had chosen out of all the tribes of Israel to put his name there. His mother’s name was Naamah the Ammonite.{h}
He did that which was evil, because he did not set his heart to seek Yahweh.

Now the acts of Rehoboam, first and last, are they not written in the words of Shemaiah the prophet and of Iddo the seer, in the matter of genealogies? There were wars between Rehoboam and Jeroboam continually.{i}
And Rehoboam slept with his fathers and was buried in the city of David, and Abijah his son reigned in his place.

notes.text: Verses 1–16 expand 1 Kings 14:21–31.
Shishak (Egyptian Sheshonq I) founded Egypt’s Twenty-second Dynasty; his own inscription at Karnak lists towns he took in Judah and Israel, about 925 B.C.
Libyans, Hebrew Lubim; Sukkiim, perhaps Libyan troops (Egyptian Tjukten) or “tent dwellers”; Cushites, people of Cush, the upper Nile region (Nubia).
Or “some deliverance.” Hebrew “as a little, deliverance.”
First Kings 14:26 adds “all the shields of gold.”
Hebrew “the runners,” the royal guard.
Or “and in Judah there were good things.” Compare 19:3.
Naamah, “pleasant”; Ammonite, of Ammon (“people” or “kinsman”). Verses 13–14 parallel 1 Kings 14:21–22.
Hebrew “to be enrolled by genealogy”; the sense is uncertain.

verses.text: In the eighteenth year of King Jeroboam, Abijah began to reign over Judah.{a}
He reigned three years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Micaiah the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. Now there was war between Abijah and Jeroboam.{b}

Abijah joined battle with an army of valiant men of war, four hundred thousand chosen men; and Jeroboam set the battle in array against him with eight hundred thousand chosen men, mighty men of valor.{c}
Then Abijah stood up on Mount Zemaraim, which is in the hill country of Ephraim, and said, “Hear me, Jeroboam and all Israel!{d}
Ought you not to know that Yahweh, the God of Israel, gave the kingdom over Israel to David forever, to him and to his sons, by a covenant of salt?{e}
Yet Jeroboam the son of Nebat, a servant of Solomon the son of David, rose up and rebelled against his lord,
and worthless men gathered about him, scoundrels, and they prevailed against Rehoboam the son of Solomon, when Rehoboam was young and fainthearted and could not stand against them.{f}
And now you think to withstand the kingdom of Yahweh in the hand of the sons of David; and you are a great multitude, and there are with you the golden calves which Jeroboam made you for gods.

Have you not driven out the priests of Yahweh, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites, and made priests for yourselves like the peoples of other lands? Whoever comes to fill his hand with a young bull and seven rams becomes a priest of what are no gods.{g}
But as for us, Yahweh is our God, and we have not forsaken him. We have priests ministering to Yahweh who are sons of Aaron, and Levites at their work.

They offer to Yahweh every morning and every evening burnt offerings and incense of sweet spices, and set out the showbread on the pure table, and tend the golden lampstand with its lamps to burn every evening; for we keep the charge of Yahweh our God, but you have forsaken him.

Behold, God is with us at our head, and his priests with their battle trumpets to sound the alarm against you. Sons of Israel, do not fight against Yahweh, the God of your fathers, for you will not succeed.”
But Jeroboam caused an ambush to come about behind them; so they were before Judah, and the ambush was behind them.
And when Judah turned, behold, the battle was before and behind them. They cried to Yahweh, and the priests blew the trumpets.
Then the men of Judah gave a shout; and as the men of Judah shouted, God struck Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah.
The children of Israel fled before Judah, and God delivered them into their hand.
Abijah and his people struck them with a great blow, and five hundred thousand chosen men of Israel fell slain.{h}
Thus the people of Israel were humbled at that time, and the people of Judah prevailed, because they relied on Yahweh, the God of their fathers.
And Abijah pursued Jeroboam and took cities from him: Bethel with its villages, Jeshanah with its villages, and Ephron with its villages.{i}
Jeroboam did not regain strength again in the days of Abijah; and Yahweh struck him down, and he died.{j}
But Abijah grew strong. He took fourteen wives and fathered twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters.
The rest of the acts of Abijah, his ways and his sayings, are written in the study of the prophet Iddo.{k}

notes.text: Verses 1–2 parallel 1 Kings 15:1–2, 6–7. Kings calls him Abijam and judges him harshly (15:3); Chronicles records his speech and victory.
Micaiah, “who is like Yahweh?”; Uriel, “God is my light”; Gibeah, “hill.” The Septuagint and 1 Kings 15:2 read Maacah, as in 11:20.
These numbers, and those of verse 17, are very large; Hebrew ’eleph, “thousand,” may in such lists denote a military unit.
Zemaraim, perhaps “two wool-heaps”; Ephraim, “doubly fruitful.”
A covenant of salt is a lasting, unbreakable covenant; compare Numbers 18:19.
Hebrew “young and tender of heart.”
“To fill his hand” is the idiom for ordaining a priest.
See verse 3 note.
Bethel, “house of God”; Jeshanah, “old.” The Ketiv reads Ephron; the Qere, Ephrain. Ephron, “fawn-like.”
First Kings 14:20 says Jeroboam reigned twenty-two years; he outlived Abijah (1 Kings 15:9). “He died” here may anticipate his later death.
Hebrew midrash, “study,” “commentary,” or “record.”

verses.text: So Abijah slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David; and Asa his son reigned in his place. In his days the land was quiet for ten years.{a}
Asa did what was good and right in the eyes of Yahweh his God.{b}
For he took away the foreign altars and the high places, broke down the pillars, and cut down the Asherim,{c}
and commanded Judah to seek Yahweh, the God of their fathers, and to do the law and the commandment.
He also took away out of all the cities of Judah the high places and the incense altars. And the kingdom had quiet before him.{d}
He built fortified cities in Judah, for the land had rest. He had no war in those years, because Yahweh had given him rest.

And he said to Judah, “Let us build these cities and surround them with walls and towers, gates and bars. The land is still before us, because we have sought Yahweh our God; we have sought him, and he has given us rest on every side.” So they built and prospered.

Asa had an army that bore bucklers and spears: out of Judah three hundred thousand, and out of Benjamin, that bore shields and drew bows, two hundred and eighty thousand; all these were mighty men of valor.
Zerah the Cushite came out against them with an army of a thousand thousands and three hundred chariots, and he came as far as Mareshah.{e}
Then Asa went out to meet him, and they set the battle in array in the Valley of Zephathah at Mareshah.{f}

And Asa cried to Yahweh his God and said, “Yahweh, there is none besides you to help, between the mighty and him who has no strength. Help us, Yahweh our God, for we rely on you, and in your name we have come against this multitude. Yahweh, you are our God; let not man prevail against you.”
So Yahweh struck the Cushites before Asa and before Judah, and the Cushites fled.

Asa and the people who were with him pursued them as far as Gerar, and so many of the Cushites fell that none remained alive, for they were broken before Yahweh and before his army. The men of Judah carried away very much plunder.{g}
And they struck all the cities around Gerar, for the dread of Yahweh was on them. They plundered all the cities, for there was much plunder in them.
They also struck the tents of those who had livestock, and carried away sheep in abundance and camels. Then they returned to Jerusalem.

notes.text: In Hebrew, 14:1 is 13:23, and 14:2–15 are 14:1–14. Asa, perhaps “healer.” Verses 1–3 parallel 1 Kings 15:8–11.
Hebrew “in the eyes of.”
Asherim, wooden poles or trees honoring the goddess Asherah.

Hebrew hammanim, perhaps incense stands; older versions, “sun images.” First Kings 15:14 and 2 Chronicles 15:17 say the high places were not removed; Chronicles may distinguish idolatrous shrines from high places used for Yahweh, or Judah from Israel.
Zerah, “rising” or “dawning”; Cushite, see 12:3. Hebrew “a thousand thousand(s)”; see 13:3 note.
Zephathah, “watchtower.” The Septuagint reads “in the valley north of Mareshah,” reflecting a different reading of the same consonants.
Gerar, “lodging place.” Or “so that they could not recover.”

verses.text: The Spirit of God came upon Azariah the son of Oded,{a}

and he went out to meet Asa and said to him, “Hear me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin: Yahweh is with you while you are with him. If you seek him, he will be found by you; but if you forsake him, he will forsake you.
For a long time Israel was without the true God, and without a teaching priest, and without law.{b}
But when in their distress they turned to Yahweh, the God of Israel, and sought him, he was found by them.
In those times there was no peace to him who went out nor to him who came in, but great troubles were on all the inhabitants of the lands.
Nation was crushed by nation, and city by city, for God troubled them with every kind of distress.
But you, be strong, and do not let your hands be slack, for there is a reward for your work.”

When Asa heard these words, the prophecy of Oded the prophet, he took courage and put away the abominations out of all the land of Judah and Benjamin, and out of the cities which he had taken from the hill country of Ephraim; and he renewed the altar of Yahweh that was before the porch of Yahweh.{c}

He gathered all Judah and Benjamin, and those who sojourned with them out of Ephraim, Manasseh, and Simeon; for they fell to him out of Israel in abundance when they saw that Yahweh his God was with him.{d}
They were gathered at Jerusalem in the third month (in May–June) of the fifteenth year of the reign of Asa.{e}
They sacrificed to Yahweh on that day, from the plunder that they had brought, seven hundred oxen and seven thousand sheep.
And they entered into a covenant to seek Yahweh, the God of their fathers, with all their heart and with all their soul,
and that whoever would not seek Yahweh, the God of Israel, should be put to death, whether small or great, whether man or woman.
They swore an oath to Yahweh with a loud voice, with shouting, with trumpets, and with horns.
And all Judah rejoiced over the oath, for they had sworn with all their heart and had sought him with their whole desire, and he was found by them; and Yahweh gave them rest all around.
King Asa also removed Maacah his mother from being queen mother, because she had made a horrid image for Asherah. Asa cut down her image, crushed it, and burned it at the Brook Kidron.{f}
But the high places were not taken away out of Israel; yet the heart of Asa was perfect all his days.{g}
He brought into the house of God the things that his father had dedicated and that he himself had dedicated, silver, gold, and vessels.
There was no more war to the thirty-fifth year of Asa’s reign.{h}

notes.text: Azariah, “Yahweh has helped”; Oded, perhaps “restorer.”
This may describe the time of the judges, or be a general warning; compare Hosea 3:4.
Hebrew “and the prophecy, Oded the prophet”; the words “Azariah the son of” may have dropped out (compare verse 1). The Septuagint also reads “Oded” (Brenton “Adad”).
Manasseh, “causing to forget”; Simeon, “hearing.”
The third month, later Sivan, counting from the spring new year; the Feast of Weeks fell in this month. The covenant oath (Hebrew shevu‘ah) may play on Shavu‘ot, “Weeks.”
Verses 16–18 parallel 1 Kings 15:13–15. Maacah, see 11:20; she was Asa’s grandmother (1 Kings 15:2, 10, “mother” in the wider sense). Kidron, perhaps “dark” or “turbid.”
Compare 14:5 note.

First Kings 16:8 places the death of Baasha (16:1) in Asa’s twenty-sixth year. The thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth years (here and 16:1) may be counted from the division of the kingdom, or the numbers may have been miscopied.

verses.text: In the thirty-sixth year of the reign of Asa, Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and built Ramah, so that he might not allow anyone to go out or come in to Asa king of Judah.{a}
Then Asa brought out silver and gold from the treasuries of the house of Yahweh and of the king’s house, and sent to Ben-hadad king of Aram, who lived in Damascus, saying,{b}

“There is a treaty between me and you, as there was between my father and your father. Behold, I am sending you silver and gold. Go, break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, that he may withdraw from me.”
Ben-hadad listened to King Asa, and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel; and they struck Ijon, Dan, Abel-maim, and all the store cities of Naphtali.{c}
When Baasha heard of it, he stopped building Ramah and let his work cease.
Then Asa the king took all Judah, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and the timber of it, with which Baasha had built; and he built Geba and Mizpah with them.{d}

At that time Hanani the seer came to Asa king of Judah and said to him, “Because you relied on the king of Aram, and did not rely on Yahweh your God, the army of the king of Aram has escaped out of your hand.{e}
Were not the Cushites and the Libyans a huge army with chariots and very many horsemen? Yet because you relied on Yahweh, he gave them into your hand.

For the eyes of Yahweh run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to show himself strong on behalf of those whose heart is wholly true to him. You have done foolishly in this, for from now on you will have wars.”
Then Asa was angry with the seer and put him in the stocks, for he was in a rage with him because of this. And Asa oppressed some of the people at the same time.{f}
The acts of Asa, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.{g}
In the thirty-ninth year of his reign Asa was diseased in his feet, and his disease became very severe; yet even in his disease he did not seek Yahweh, but the physicians.{h}
And Asa slept with his fathers, dying in the forty-first year of his reign.

They buried him in his own tomb, which he had hewn out for himself in the city of David, and laid him in the bed which was filled with sweet odors and various kinds of spices prepared by the perfumers’ art; and they made a very great burning for him.{i}

notes.text: Verses 1–6 parallel 1 Kings 15:16–22. Baasha, meaning uncertain; Ramah, “height.” See 15:19 note.
Ben-hadad, “son of Hadad,” the storm god; Aram, see 1:17; Damascus, meaning uncertain.
Ijon, perhaps “ruin”; Abel-maim, “meadow of waters” (1 Kings 15:20 Abel-beth-maacah); Naphtali, “my wrestling.”
Geba, “hill”; Mizpah, “watchtower.”
Hanani, “gracious.” Verses 7–10 are not in Kings.
Hebrew “the house of the stocks.”
Compare 1 Kings 15:23–24.
Or “but sought the physicians”; perhaps a play on Asa’s name if it means “healer.”
The fire was a burning of spices in his honor, not a cremation; compare 21:19; Jeremiah 34:5.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat his son reigned in his place and strengthened himself against Israel.{a}
He placed forces in all the fortified cities of Judah, and set garrisons in the land of Judah and in the cities of Ephraim that Asa his father had taken.
Yahweh was with Jehoshaphat, because he walked in the earlier ways of his father David, and did not seek the Baals,{b}
but sought the God of his father and walked in his commandments, and not according to the deeds of Israel.
Therefore Yahweh established the kingdom in his hand. All Judah brought tribute to Jehoshaphat, and he had riches and honor in abundance.
His heart was lifted up in the ways of Yahweh; and moreover he took away the high places and the Asherim out of Judah.{c}
In the third year of his reign he sent his princes, Ben-hail, Obadiah, Zechariah, Nethanel, and Micaiah, to teach in the cities of Judah;{d}
and with them the Levites Shemaiah, Nethaniah, Zebadiah, Asahel, Shemiramoth, Jehonathan, Adonijah, Tobijah, and Tob-adonijah; and with them Elishama and Jehoram the priests.{e}
They taught in Judah, having the book of the law of Yahweh with them. They went about through all the cities of Judah and taught among the people.
The dread of Yahweh fell on all the kingdoms of the lands that were around Judah, and they made no war against Jehoshaphat.
Some of the Philistines brought Jehoshaphat presents and silver as tribute, and the Arabians also brought him flocks: seven thousand seven hundred rams and seven thousand seven hundred male goats.
Jehoshaphat grew great exceedingly; and he built castles and store cities in Judah.
and he had much work in the cities of Judah; and he had men of war, mighty men of valor, in Jerusalem.
This is the muster of them by their fathers’ houses: Of Judah, the captains of thousands: Adnah the captain, and with him three hundred thousand mighty men of valor;{f}
and next to him Jehohanan the captain, and with him two hundred and eighty thousand;{g}
and next to him Amasiah the son of Zichri, who offered himself willingly to Yahweh, and with him two hundred thousand mighty men of valor.{h}
Of Benjamin: Eliada, a mighty man of valor, and with him two hundred thousand armed with bow and shield;{i}
and next to him Jehozabad, and with him a hundred and eighty thousand ready for war.{j}
These were those who served the king, besides those whom the king had put in the fortified cities throughout all Judah.

notes.text: Jehoshaphat, “Yahweh has judged.” Compare 1 Kings 15:24; 22:41–50.
The Septuagint and some Hebrew manuscripts lack “David,” giving “the earlier ways of his father,” that is, Asa. Baals, local forms of the god Baal (“lord, owner”).
Hebrew “his heart was high,” here in a good sense, “he took courage.” Contrast 20:33.
Ben-hail, “son of strength” (or read “his princes, men of valor”); Obadiah, “servant of Yahweh”; Zechariah, “Yahweh remembers”; Nethanel, “God has given”; Micaiah, see 13:2.

Shemaiah, see 11:2; Nethaniah, “Yahweh has given”; Zebadiah, “Yahweh has bestowed”; Asahel, “God has made”; Shemiramoth, perhaps “name of heights”; Jehonathan, “Yahweh has given”; Adonijah, “my lord is Yahweh”; Tobijah, “Yahweh is good”; Tob-adonijah, “good is my lord Yahweh”; Elishama, “God has heard”; Jehoram, “Yahweh is exalted.”
Adnah, “pleasure.” The total of verses 14–18 (1,160,000) is very large; see 13:3 note.
Jehohanan, “Yahweh is gracious.”
Amasiah, “Yahweh carries”; Zichri, “remembered.”
Eliada, “God knows.”
Jehozabad, “Yahweh has bestowed.”

verses.text: Now Jehoshaphat had riches and honor in abundance, and he made a marriage alliance with Ahab.{a}
After some years he went down to Ahab in Samaria. Ahab slaughtered sheep and oxen in abundance for him and for the people who were with him, and urged him to go up against Ramoth-gilead.{b}
Ahab king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat king of Judah, “Will you go with me to Ramoth-gilead?” He answered him, “I am as you are, and my people as your people; we will be with you in the war.”
And Jehoshaphat said to the king of Israel, “Inquire first, I pray you, for the word of Yahweh.”

Then the king of Israel gathered the prophets together, four hundred men, and said to them, “Shall we go to Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall I forbear?” They said, “Go up, for God will give it into the hand of the king.”
But Jehoshaphat said, “Is there not here another prophet of Yahweh, that we may inquire of him?”

The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “There is yet one man by whom we may inquire of Yahweh, but I hate him, for he never prophesies good concerning me, but always evil. He is Micaiah the son of Imla.” And Jehoshaphat said, “Let not the king say so.”{c}
Then the king of Israel called an officer and said, “Bring quickly Micaiah the son of Imla.”{d}

Now the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat king of Judah were sitting each on his throne, clothed in their robes; they sat at the threshing floor at the entrance of the gate of Samaria, and all the prophets were prophesying before them.{e}
Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah made himself horns of iron and said, “Thus says Yahweh: ‘With these you shall push the Arameans until they are consumed.’”{f}
All the prophets prophesied so, saying, “Go up to Ramoth-gilead and prosper, for Yahweh will give it into the hand of the king.”

The messenger who went to call Micaiah spoke to him, saying, “Behold, the words of the prophets declare good to the king with one mouth. Let your word, I pray you, be like one of theirs, and speak good.”
And Micaiah said, “As Yahweh lives, what my God says, that will I speak.”
When he had come to the king, the king said to him, “Micaiah, shall we go to Ramoth-gilead to battle, or shall I forbear?” And he said, “Go up and prosper; they shall be given into your hand.”
The king said to him, “How many times shall I adjure you that you speak to me nothing but the truth in the name of Yahweh?”
And he said, “I saw all Israel scattered on the mountains, as sheep that have no shepherd. And Yahweh said, ‘These have no master; let them return each to his house in peace.’”
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “Did I not tell you that he would not prophesy good concerning me, but evil?”
And Micaiah said, “Therefore hear the word of Yahweh: I saw Yahweh sitting on his throne, and all the host of heaven standing on his right hand and on his left.
And Yahweh said, ‘Who will entice Ahab king of Israel, that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?’ And one said this, and another said that.
Then a spirit came forth and stood before Yahweh and said, ‘I will entice him.’ And Yahweh said to him, ‘By what means?’{g}
And he said, ‘I will go forth and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.’ And he said, ‘You shall entice him, and you shall also prevail; go forth and do so.’
Now therefore, behold, Yahweh has put a lying spirit in the mouth of these your prophets, and Yahweh has spoken evil concerning you.”
Then Zedekiah the son of Chenaanah came near and struck Micaiah on the cheek and said, “Which way did the Spirit of Yahweh go from me to speak to you?”
And Micaiah said, “Behold, you shall see on that day, when you go into an inner chamber to hide yourself.”
And the king of Israel said, “Take Micaiah, and carry him back to Amon the governor of the city and to Joash the king’s son,{h}
and say, ‘Thus says the king: Put this fellow in the prison, and feed him with bread of affliction and with water of affliction, until I return in peace.’”{i}
And Micaiah said, “If you return at all in peace, Yahweh has not spoken by me.” And he said, “Hear, you peoples, all of you.”{j}
So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth-gilead.
The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “I will disguise myself and go into the battle, but you put on your robes.” So the king of Israel disguised himself, and they went into the battle.
Now the king of Aram had commanded the captains of his chariots, saying, “Fight neither with small nor great, but only with the king of Israel.”

When the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, they said, “It is the king of Israel.” So they turned about to fight against him. But Jehoshaphat cried out, and Yahweh helped him; God drew them away from him.{k}
When the captains of the chariots saw that it was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him.

But a certain man drew his bow at random and struck the king of Israel between the joints of the armor. So he said to the driver of the chariot, “Turn your hand and carry me out of the army, for I am badly wounded.”{l}
The battle grew fierce that day, and the king of Israel held himself up in his chariot facing the Arameans until evening; and about the time of the going down of the sun he died.{m}

notes.text: Ahab, “father’s brother.” The marriage was of Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat to Athaliah daughter of Ahab (21:6; 22:2). Chapter 18 closely parallels 1 Kings 22:1–35.
Samaria, “watch post”; Ramoth-gilead, “heights of Gilead.”
Micaiah, “who is like Yahweh?”; Imla, “he fills.”
The Ketiv spells the name Micaihu, a longer form.
Or “in an open place.” Zedekiah (next verse) and the prophets performed before the two kings.
Zedekiah, “Yahweh is righteousness”; Chenaanah, perhaps “merchant” or “Canaanitess.”
Hebrew “With what?”
Amon, “faithful” or “master workman”; Joash, perhaps “Yahweh has given.”
That is, meager prison rations.
