The same words open the book of the prophet Micah (Micah 1:2). They are absent from the Septuagint of 1 Kings 22:28 but present in Hebrew Kings and here.
“And Yahweh helped him; God drew them away” is not in 1 Kings 22:32.
The Ketiv reads “your hands,” the Qere “your hand.” Hebrew “out of the camp.”
First Kings 22:35–38 adds that the blood ran into the chariot and that dogs licked it up at Samaria.

verses.text: And Jehoshaphat the king of Judah returned to his house in Jerusalem in peace.

But Jehu the son of Hanani the seer went out to meet him and said to King Jehoshaphat, “Should you help the wicked and love those who hate Yahweh? Because of this, wrath has gone out against you from Yahweh.{a}
Nevertheless, there are good things found in you, in that you have removed the Asheroth out of the land, and have set your heart to seek God.”{b}
Jehoshaphat dwelt at Jerusalem. And he went out again among the people, from Beersheba to the hill country of Ephraim, and brought them back to Yahweh, the God of their fathers.{c}
He appointed judges in the land in all the fortified cities of Judah, city by city,{d}
and said to the judges, “Consider what you do, for you judge not for man but for Yahweh, and he is with you in giving judgment.
Now then, let the fear of Yahweh be upon you. Take heed what you do, for there is no injustice with Yahweh our God, nor respect of persons, nor taking of bribes.”

Moreover in Jerusalem Jehoshaphat appointed some of the Levites and priests and heads of fathers’ houses of Israel, to give judgment for Yahweh and to decide disputes. And they returned to Jerusalem.{e}
And he charged them, saying, “Thus you shall do in the fear of Yahweh, faithfully, and with a perfect heart.

Whenever any controversy comes to you from your brothers who dwell in their cities, between blood and blood, between law and commandment, statutes and ordinances, you shall warn them, that they not be guilty toward Yahweh, and so wrath come upon you and upon your brothers. This do, and you shall not be guilty.{f}

And behold, Amariah the chief priest is over you in all matters of Yahweh; and Zebadiah the son of Ishmael, the ruler of the house of Judah, in all the king’s matters; and the Levites will be officers before you. Deal courageously, and may Yahweh be with the good.”{g}

notes.text: Jehu, “Yahweh is he”; Hanani, see 16:7.
Asheroth, plural of Asherah; see 14:3 note.
Beersheba, “well of seven” or “well of the oath.” Jehoshaphat’s name, “Yahweh has judged,” suits his judicial reform (verses 5–11).
Compare Deuteronomy 16:18–20; 17:8–13.
The Septuagint reads “to judge the inhabitants of Jerusalem,” a different vocalization of “they returned” (Hebrew vayyashuvu, read as yoshvei, “inhabitants of”).
“Between blood and blood,” that is, cases of homicide and bloodshed.
Amariah, “Yahweh has said”; Zebadiah, see 17:8; Ishmael, “God hears.”

verses.text: After this the children of Moab and the children of Ammon, and with them some of the Meunites, came against Jehoshaphat to battle.{a}
Some men came and told Jehoshaphat, “A great multitude is coming against you from beyond the sea, from Aram; and behold, they are in Hazazon-tamar” (that is, En-gedi).{b}
Then Jehoshaphat was afraid and set his face to seek Yahweh, and proclaimed a fast throughout all Judah.
And Judah gathered together to seek help from Yahweh; from all the cities of Judah they came to seek Yahweh.
And Jehoshaphat stood in the assembly of Judah and Jerusalem, in the house of Yahweh, before the new court,

and said, “O Yahweh, the God of our fathers, are not you God in heaven? And are not you ruler over all the kingdoms of the nations? Power and might are in your hand, so that none is able to withstand you.
Did you not, our God, drive out the inhabitants of this land before your people Israel, and give it forever to the seed of Abraham your friend?{c}
And they have dwelt in it and have built you a sanctuary in it for your name, saying,

‘If evil comes upon us, the sword, judgment, or pestilence, or famine, we will stand before this house and before you, for your name is in this house, and cry to you in our affliction, and you will hear and save.’{d}
And now, behold, the men of Ammon and Moab and Mount Seir, whom you would not let Israel invade when they came from the land of Egypt, but they turned aside from them and did not destroy them,{e}
behold, they reward us by coming to cast us out of your possession, which you have given us to inherit.
O our God, will you not judge them? For we have no might against this great company that comes against us; neither know we what to do, but our eyes are upon you.”
And all Judah stood before Yahweh, with their little ones, their wives, and their children.
Then the Spirit of Yahweh came upon Jahaziel the son of Zechariah, the son of Benaiah, the son of Jeiel, the son of Mattaniah, a Levite of the sons of Asaph, in the midst of the assembly.{f}

and he said, “Hearken, all Judah, and you inhabitants of Jerusalem, and you King Jehoshaphat: Yahweh says this to you, ‘Do not be afraid, and do not be dismayed by reason of this great multitude, for the battle is not yours but God’s.
Tomorrow go down against them. Behold, they will come up by the ascent of Ziz. You will find them at the end of the valley, east of the wilderness of Jeruel.{g}

You shall not need to fight in this battle. Set yourselves, stand still, and see the salvation of Yahweh with you, O Judah and Jerusalem.’ Fear not, nor be dismayed; tomorrow go out against them, for Yahweh is with you.”{h}
Then Jehoshaphat bowed his head with his face to the ground, and all Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem fell down before Yahweh, worshiping Yahweh.
And the Levites, of the sons of the Kohathites and of the sons of the Korahites, stood up to praise Yahweh, the God of Israel, with a very loud voice.{i}

They rose early in the morning and went out into the wilderness of Tekoa. And as they went out, Jehoshaphat stood and said, “Hear me, Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem: Believe in Yahweh your God, and you will be established; believe his prophets, and you will prosper.”{j}

When he had taken counsel with the people, he appointed those who should sing to Yahweh and praise the splendor of holiness, as they went out before the army, and say, “Give thanks to Yahweh, for his steadfast love endures forever.”{k}
And when they began to sing and to praise, Yahweh set ambushes against the men of Ammon, Moab, and Mount Seir, who had come against Judah, and they were struck down.

For the children of Ammon and Moab stood up against the inhabitants of Mount Seir, utterly to slay and destroy them; and when they had made an end of the inhabitants of Seir, everyone helped to destroy another.
When Judah came to the watchtower of the wilderness, they looked upon the multitude; and behold, they were dead bodies fallen to the earth, and there were none that escaped.

When Jehoshaphat and his people came to take the plunder of them, they found among them in abundance goods and corpses and precious things, which they stripped off for themselves, more than they could carry away; and they were three days in taking the plunder, it was so much.{l}
On the fourth day they assembled in the Valley of Beracah, for there they blessed Yahweh. Therefore the name of that place has been called the Valley of Beracah to this day.{m}
Then they returned, every man of Judah and Jerusalem, with Jehoshaphat at their head, returning to Jerusalem with joy, for Yahweh had made them rejoice over their enemies.
They came to Jerusalem with psalteries and harps and trumpets, to the house of Yahweh.
And the fear of God came on all the kingdoms of the countries when they heard that Yahweh had fought against the enemies of Israel.
So the realm of Jehoshaphat was quiet, for his God gave him rest all around.
Thus Jehoshaphat reigned over Judah. He was thirty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-five years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Azubah the daughter of Shilhi.{n}
He walked in the way of Asa his father and departed not from it, doing that which was right in the eyes of Yahweh.
However, the high places were not taken away; neither as yet had the people set their hearts on the God of their fathers.{o}
Now the rest of the acts of Jehoshaphat, first and last, behold, they are written in the words of Jehu the son of Hanani, which are recorded in the book of the kings of Israel.
After this Jehoshaphat king of Judah joined himself with Ahaziah king of Israel, who did very wickedly.{p}
And he joined himself with him to make ships to go to Tarshish; and they made the ships in Ezion-geber.{q}

Then Eliezer the son of Dodavahu of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying, “Because you have joined yourself with Ahaziah, Yahweh has broken up your works.” And the ships were wrecked and were not able to go to Tarshish.{r}

notes.text: Hebrew “some of the Ammonites,” which repeats the Ammonites just named; the Septuagint reads “Minaeans,” that is, Meunites (compare 26:7). Moab, see 1 Chronicles 1:46 note; Ammon, “people.”

Hebrew and Septuagint “from Aram”; many scholars read “from Edom” (the Hebrew letters d and r are easily confused), since the invaders came from the south around the Dead Sea (“the sea”). Hazazon-tamar, perhaps “gravel bed of the palm”; En-gedi, “spring of the young goat.”
Compare Isaiah 41:8; James 2:23.
Compare Solomon’s prayer, 6:28–30.
Seir, “hairy” or “shaggy,” the hill country of Edom. Compare Deuteronomy 2:4–19.
Jahaziel, “God sees”; Benaiah, “Yahweh has built”; Jeiel, meaning uncertain; Mattaniah, “gift of Yahweh”; Asaph, “gatherer.”
Ziz, perhaps “blossom”; Jeruel, perhaps “founded by God.” Hebrew “before,” that is, facing east.
Compare Exodus 14:13.
Kohathites, from Kohath (“assembly”?); Korahites, from Korah (“baldness”).
Tekoa, perhaps “trumpet blast.” “Believe … be established” plays on two forms of the Hebrew verb ’aman; compare Isaiah 7:9.
Or “in holy attire.” “Steadfast love,” Hebrew hesed.
Hebrew “corpses” (pegarim); some scholars read “garments” (begadim), which differs by one letter. The Septuagint reads “cattle and furniture and spoils.”
Beracah, “blessing.”
Verses 31–34 parallel 1 Kings 22:41–45. Azubah, “forsaken”; Shilhi, perhaps “sent.”

First Kings 22:43 says the people still sacrificed and burned incense on the high places. Compare 17:6, where Jehoshaphat removed high places; the two statements may concern different kinds of shrines or stages of the reign.
Ahaziah, “Yahweh has grasped.” Or “and he (Jehoshaphat) did very wickedly in doing so.”

Tarshish, a distant western port; compare 9:21 note. First Kings 22:48–49 says Jehoshaphat built “ships of Tarshish” (a type of large seagoing ship) to go to Ophir for gold, and that he refused Ahaziah’s offer to partner in the venture. Chronicles may have read “ships of Tarshish” as ships going to Tarshish; Ezion-geber lay on the Red Sea, not the Mediterranean. Ezion-geber, perhaps “backbone of a man.”
Eliezer, “God is help”; Dodavahu, “beloved of Yahweh.” This prophecy is not in Kings.

verses.text: Jehoshaphat slept with his fathers and was buried with his fathers in the city of David, and Jehoram his son reigned in his place.{a}
He had brothers, the sons of Jehoshaphat: Azariah, Jehiel, Zechariah, Azariahu, Michael, and Shephatiah; all these were the sons of Jehoshaphat king of Israel.{b}
Their father gave them great gifts of silver, gold, and precious things, with fortified cities in Judah; but he gave the kingdom to Jehoram, because he was the firstborn.
When Jehoram had risen up over the kingdom of his father and had made himself strong, he killed all his brothers with the sword, and also some of the princes of Israel.
Jehoram was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned eight years in Jerusalem.{c}
He walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as did the house of Ahab, for he had the daughter of Ahab as wife; and he did that which was evil in the sight of Yahweh.
Yet Yahweh would not destroy the house of David, because of the covenant that he had made with David, and since he had promised to give a lamp to him and to his sons forever.{d}
In his days Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah and made a king over themselves.
Then Jehoram passed over with his captains and all his chariots with him; and he rose up by night and struck the Edomites who had surrounded him and the captains of the chariots.{e}
So Edom revolted from under the hand of Judah to this day. At that same time Libnah also revolted from under his hand, because he had forsaken Yahweh, the God of his fathers.{f}
Moreover, he made high places in the hill country of Judah, and caused the inhabitants of Jerusalem to commit fornication, and led Judah astray.{g}

And a letter came to him from Elijah the prophet, saying, “Thus says Yahweh, the God of David your father: ‘Because you have not walked in the ways of Jehoshaphat your father, or in the ways of Asa king of Judah,{h}

but have walked in the way of the kings of Israel, and have made Judah and the inhabitants of Jerusalem to commit fornication, as the house of Ahab did, and also have killed your brothers of your father’s house, who were better than you,
behold, Yahweh will strike with a great blow your people, your sons, your wives, and all your goods,
and you shall have great sickness by disease of your bowels, until your bowels fall out by reason of the sickness, day by day.’”
And Yahweh stirred up against Jehoram the spirit of the Philistines and of the Arabians who are near the Cushites;{i}

and they came up against Judah, broke into it, and carried away all the goods that were found in the king’s house, and also his sons and his wives, so that there was not a son left to him except Jehoahaz, his youngest son.{j}
And after all this Yahweh struck him in his bowels with a disease for which there was no healing.
In the course of time, at the end of two years, his bowels came out because of his disease, and he died in severe pain. His people made no burning for him, like the burning for his fathers.{k}

He was thirty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned in Jerusalem eight years; and he departed without being desired. They buried him in the city of David, but not in the sepulchres of the kings.{l}

notes.text: Jehoram, “Yahweh is exalted”; also Joram. Verses 1 and 5–10 parallel 2 Kings 8:16–22.

Azariah, “Yahweh has helped” (twice, in slightly different Hebrew forms); Jehiel, “God lives”; Michael, “who is like God?”; Shephatiah, “Yahweh has judged.” “King of Israel” here means king of Judah, the true Israel in Chronicles’ view; the Septuagint reads “king of Judah.”
Jehoram may have reigned for some years alongside his father (compare 2 Kings 1:17; 3:1; 8:16).
Hebrew “a lamp,” a living descendant on the throne; compare 1 Kings 11:36.
Second Kings 8:21 says Joram went over to Zair, and that his army fled home; the outcome was an escape, not a victory.
Libnah, “whiteness,” a town in the Shephelah near Philistia.
The Septuagint reads “in the cities of Judah.” “Commit fornication,” that is, be unfaithful to Yahweh by idolatry.

Elijah, “my God is Yahweh.” Elijah is not otherwise linked with Jehoram of Judah, and 2 Kings 2–3 seems to place Elijah’s departure before Jehoram’s reign (Elisha is active under Jehoshaphat, 2 Kings 3:11). The letter may have been written beforehand, or Elijah may have lived into the early years of Jehoram’s coregency; the matter is debated.
Cush, see 12:3.
Jehoahaz, “Yahweh has grasped,” the same elements as Ahaziah (22:1) in reverse order.
Hebrew “in severe diseases.” On the burning, see 16:14 note.
Not in the tombs of the kings: this detail is not in Kings (compare 2 Kings 8:24).

verses.text: The inhabitants of Jerusalem made Ahaziah his youngest son king in his place; for the band of men that came with the Arabians to the camp had slain all the eldest. So Ahaziah the son of Jehoram king of Judah reigned.{a}
Ahaziah was forty-two years old when he began to reign, and he reigned one year in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Athaliah, the granddaughter of Omri.{b}
He also walked in the ways of the house of Ahab, for his mother was his counselor in doing wickedly.
He did that which was evil in the sight of Yahweh, as did the house of Ahab; for they were his counselors after the death of his father, to his destruction.
He also walked after their counsel, and went with Jehoram the son of Ahab king of Israel to make war against Hazael king of Aram at Ramoth-gilead; and the Arameans wounded Joram.{c}

And he returned to be healed in Jezreel of the wounds that they had given him at Ramah, when he fought against Hazael king of Aram. And Azariah the son of Jehoram king of Judah went down to see Jehoram the son of Ahab in Jezreel, because he was sick.{d}

Now the destruction of Ahaziah was of God, in that he went to Joram; for when he had come, he went out with Jehoram against Jehu the son of Nimshi, whom Yahweh had anointed to cut off the house of Ahab.{e}
And when Jehu was executing judgment on the house of Ahab, he found the princes of Judah and the sons of Ahaziah’s brothers who served Ahaziah, and he killed them.{f}

He sought Ahaziah, and they caught him (now he was hiding in Samaria), and they brought him to Jehu and slew him; and they buried him, for they said, “He is the son of Jehoshaphat, who sought Yahweh with all his heart.” And the house of Ahaziah had no power to hold the kingdom.{g}
Now when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal seed of the house of Judah.{h}

But Jehoshabeath, the king’s daughter, took Joash the son of Ahaziah and stole him away from among the king’s sons who were being put to death, and she put him and his nurse in a bedroom. Thus Jehoshabeath, the daughter of King Jehoram and wife of Jehoiada the priest, because she was the sister of Ahaziah, hid him from Athaliah, so that she did not put him to death.{i}
He was with them hidden in the house of God six years, and Athaliah reigned over the land.

notes.text: Ahaziah, “Yahweh has grasped”; also called Jehoahaz (21:17). Verses 1–6 parallel 2 Kings 8:24–29.

Hebrew “forty-two,” which is impossible if his father died at forty (21:20). Second Kings 8:26 reads “twenty-two,” and the Septuagint here reads “twenty.” Athaliah, “Yahweh is exalted”; Omri, meaning uncertain. Hebrew “daughter,” in the wider sense; she was Ahab’s daughter (21:6).
Hazael, “God sees.”
Ramah, short for Ramoth-gilead. Hebrew “Azariah”; the Septuagint and 2 Kings 8:29 read “Ahaziah,” which is surely meant (compare verses 1, 7). Jezreel, “God sows.”
Jehu, see 19:2; Nimshi, perhaps “weasel.” Compare 2 Kings 9–10.
Second Kings 10:12–14 calls them “the brothers of Ahaziah” and gives their number as forty-two.

Second Kings 9:27–28 says that Ahaziah, wounded near Ibleam, fled to Megiddo and died there, and that his servants carried him to Jerusalem for burial. Chronicles summarizes differently; the accounts may reflect different sources or stages of his flight.
Verses 10–12 parallel 2 Kings 11:1–3.
Jehoshabeath, “Yahweh is an oath” (2 Kings 11:2 Jehosheba); Joash, see 18:25; Jehoiada, “Yahweh knows.” That she was the wife of Jehoiada is stated only in Chronicles.

verses.text: In the seventh year Jehoiada strengthened himself and took the captains of hundreds into covenant with him: Azariah the son of Jeroham, Ishmael the son of Jehohanan, Azariah the son of Obed, Maaseiah the son of Adaiah, and Elishaphat the son of Zichri.{a}
And they went about through Judah and gathered the Levites from all the cities of Judah, and the heads of fathers’ houses of Israel, and they came to Jerusalem.
And all the assembly made a covenant with the king in the house of God. And Jehoiada said to them, “Behold, the king’s son shall reign, as Yahweh spoke concerning the sons of David.
This is the thing that you shall do: a third part of you that come in on the Sabbath, of the priests and of the Levites, shall be porters of the thresholds,{b}
and a third part shall be at the king’s house, and a third part at the Gate of the Foundation; and all the people shall be in the courts of the house of Yahweh.{c}
But let none come into the house of Yahweh, save the priests and they that minister of the Levites; they shall come in, for they are holy; but all the people shall keep the charge of Yahweh.{d}
The Levites shall surround the king, every man with his weapons in his hand; and whoever enters the house, let him be put to death. Be with the king when he comes in and when he goes out.”

So the Levites and all Judah did according to all that Jehoiada the priest commanded. They each took his men, those who were to come in on the Sabbath, with those who were to go out on the Sabbath, for Jehoiada the priest did not dismiss the divisions.
And Jehoiada the priest delivered to the captains of hundreds the spears and the large and small shields that had been King David’s, which were in the house of God.
And he set all the people, every man with his weapon in his hand, from the right side of the house to the left side of the house, along the altar and the house, around the king.
Then they brought out the king’s son and put the crown on him and gave him the testimony, and made him king; and Jehoiada and his sons anointed him, and they said, “Long live the king!”{e}
When Athaliah heard the noise of the people running and praising the king, she came to the people into the house of Yahweh.

And she looked, and behold, the king was standing by his pillar at the entrance, and the captains and the trumpeters beside the king, and all the people of the land rejoicing and blowing trumpets, and the singers with their instruments of music leading the praise. And Athaliah tore her clothes and cried, “Treason! Treason!”{f}

Jehoiada the priest brought out the captains of hundreds who were set over the army, and said to them, “Bring her out between the ranks; and whoever follows her, let him be slain with the sword.” For the priest said, “Slay her not in the house of Yahweh.”
So they made way for her; and she went to the entrance of the Horse Gate to the king’s house, and they slew her there.{g}
And Jehoiada made a covenant between himself and all the people and the king, that they should be Yahweh’s people.
All the people went to the house of Baal and broke it down, and broke his altars and his images in pieces, and slew Mattan the priest of Baal before the altars.{h}

Jehoiada appointed the offices of the house of Yahweh under the hand of the priests the Levites, whom David had distributed in the house of Yahweh, to offer the burnt offerings of Yahweh, as it is written in the law of Moses, with rejoicing and with singing, as David had ordained.
He stationed the gatekeepers at the gates of the house of Yahweh, so that no one who was unclean in anything should enter.

And he took the captains of hundreds, the nobles, the governors of the people, and all the people of the land, and they brought the king down from the house of Yahweh, marching through the upper gate to the king’s house; and they set the king on the throne of the kingdom.
So all the people of the land rejoiced, and the city was quiet; and they had slain Athaliah with the sword.

notes.text: Chapter 23 parallels 2 Kings 11:4–20; Chronicles names the five captains and gives a larger role to the Levites. Azariah, see 15:1; Jeroham, “he is shown compassion”; Ishmael, see 19:11; Jehohanan, see 17:15; Obed, “servant”; Maaseiah, “work of Yahweh”; Adaiah, “Yahweh has adorned”; Elishaphat, “God has judged”; Zichri, see 17:16.
Hebrew “of the thresholds,” that is, the temple entrances.
Second Kings 11:6 reads “the Gate of Sur.”
That is, stay in the outer courts as Yahweh requires.
“The testimony,” perhaps a copy of the covenant law (compare Deuteronomy 17:18), or a royal document.
Hebrew “Conspiracy! Conspiracy!”
Hebrew “made two sides for her,” that is, made way for her or seized her.
Mattan, “gift.”

verses.text: Joash was seven years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Zibiah of Beersheba.{a}
And Joash did what was right in the eyes of Yahweh all the days of Jehoiada the priest.
Jehoiada took for him two wives, and he fathered sons and daughters.
After this Joash decided to restore the house of Yahweh.{b}

And he gathered the priests and the Levites and said to them, “Go out to the cities of Judah and gather from all Israel money to repair the house of your God from year to year, and see that you hasten the matter.” But the Levites did not hasten it.

The king called for Jehoiada the chief, and said to him, “Why have you not required of the Levites to bring in out of Judah and out of Jerusalem the tax of Moses the servant of Yahweh, and of the assembly of Israel, for the tent of the testimony?”{c}
For the sons of Athaliah, that wicked woman, had broken into the house of God, and had also used all the holy things of the house of Yahweh for the Baals.{d}
So the king commanded, and they made a chest and set it outside the gate of the house of Yahweh.
And proclamation was made throughout Judah and Jerusalem to bring in for Yahweh the tax that Moses the servant of God laid on Israel in the wilderness.
All the princes and all the people rejoiced, and brought in, and cast into the chest, until they had made an end.

Whenever the chest was brought to the king’s officers by the hand of the Levites, and when they saw that there was much money, the king’s scribe and the chief priest’s officer came and emptied the chest, and took it and carried it to its place again. Thus they did day by day, and gathered money in abundance.

And the king and Jehoiada gave it to those who had charge of the work of the house of Yahweh, and they hired masons and carpenters to restore the house of Yahweh, and also workers in iron and bronze to repair the house of Yahweh.
So the workmen wrought, and the work of repairing went forward in their hands; and they set up the house of God in its state, and strengthened it.

When they had finished, they brought the rest of the money before the king and Jehoiada, of which were made vessels for the house of Yahweh, vessels to minister and to offer, and spoons, and vessels of gold and silver. And they offered burnt offerings in the house of Yahweh continually all the days of Jehoiada.{e}
But Jehoiada grew old and full of days, and he died; he was a hundred and thirty years old at his death.{f}
And they buried him in the city of David among the kings, because he had done good in Israel, and toward God and his house.
Now after the death of Jehoiada the princes of Judah came and paid homage to the king. Then the king listened to them.
And they forsook the house of Yahweh, the God of their fathers, and served the Asherim and the idols. And wrath came upon Judah and Jerusalem for this guilt of theirs.
Yet he sent prophets among them to bring them back to Yahweh. These testified against them, but they would not give ear.

Then the Spirit of God clothed Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest; and he stood above the people and said to them, “God says this: ‘Why do you disobey the commandments of Yahweh, so that you cannot prosper? Because you have forsaken Yahweh, he has also forsaken you.’”{g}
They conspired against him, and stoned him with stones at the commandment of the king in the court of the house of Yahweh.
Thus Joash the king remembered not the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done to him, but slew his son. And when he died, he said, “Yahweh look upon it and require it.”{h}

At the turn of the year the army of the Arameans came up against Joash. They came to Judah and Jerusalem and destroyed all the princes of the people from among the people, and sent all their spoil to the king of Damascus.{i}

For the army of the Arameans came with a small company of men, and Yahweh delivered a very great army into their hand, because they had forsaken Yahweh, the God of their fathers. So they executed judgment upon Joash.

When they were departed from him (for they left him very sick), his own servants conspired against him for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest, and slew him on his bed, and he died. They buried him in the city of David, but they buried him not in the sepulchres of the kings.{j}
Those who conspired against him were Zabad the son of Shimeath the Ammonitess, and Jehozabad the son of Shimrith the Moabitess.{k}

Concerning his sons, and the many oracles against him, and the rebuilding of the house of God, behold, they are written in the commentary on the book of the kings. And Amaziah his son reigned in his place.{l}

notes.text: Joash, also Jehoash; see 18:25. Zibiah, “gazelle.” Verses 1–14 parallel 2 Kings 12:1–16, which describes the collection somewhat differently.
Hebrew “it was in the heart of Joash.”
Compare Exodus 30:12–16, the half-shekel tax (about 0.2 ounce, 5.7 grams of silver).
Hebrew “her sons”; perhaps her followers. Or “had broken up the house of God.”
Hebrew “spoons,” small vessels or pans for incense. Second Kings 12:13 says the money was not used for vessels; Chronicles may refer to the surplus after repairs.
Jehoiada’s age (130) exceeds that of Moses and Aaron.

Hebrew “clothed himself with Zechariah”; compare Judges 6:34. Zechariah, see 17:7. Jesus appears to refer to this martyrdom in Matthew 23:35 and Luke 11:51, where Matthew calls him “son of Barachiah” (compare Zechariah 1:1).
Or “May Yahweh see and avenge.” Jehoiada was Zechariah’s father. Compare 2 Kings 12:17–18, which describes the Aramean threat and tribute.
That is, in the spring, when kings went to war (1 Chronicles 20:1).
Hebrew “sons”; the Septuagint reads “son.” Second Kings 12:20–21 places his death at the house of Millo.

Zabad, “he has bestowed” (2 Kings 12:21 Jozacar, “Yahweh has remembered”); Shimeath, “hearing”; Jehozabad, see 17:18; Shimrith, “guardian” (2 Kings 12:21 Shomer, “guardian,” a man’s name). Ammonitess and Moabitess are not in Kings.
The Ketiv and Qere differ slightly in spelling the word for “many.” Amaziah, “Yahweh is strong.”

verses.text: Amaziah was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned twenty-nine years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jehoaddan of Jerusalem.{a}
He did that which was right in the eyes of Yahweh, yet not with a perfect heart.
Now when the kingdom was established to him, he slew his servants who had slain the king his father.

But he did not put their children to death, but did according to that which is written in the law in the book of Moses, as Yahweh commanded, saying, “The fathers shall not die for the children, nor shall the children die for the fathers; but every man shall die for his own sin.”{b}

Moreover Amaziah gathered Judah together and ordered them according to their fathers’ houses, under captains of thousands and captains of hundreds, all Judah and Benjamin. He numbered them from twenty years old and upward, and found them three hundred thousand chosen men, able to go forth to war, that could handle spear and shield.
He hired also a hundred thousand mighty men of valor out of Israel for about three and three-quarter tons of silver.{c}
But there came a man of God to him, saying, “O king, let not the army of Israel go with you; for Yahweh is not with Israel, with all the children of Ephraim.
But if you will go, do it, be strong for the battle; God will cast you down before the enemy, for God has power to help and to cast down.”{d}
Amaziah said to the man of God, “But what shall we do for the silver which I have given to the troops of Israel?” And the man of God answered, “Yahweh is able to give you much more than this.”
Then Amaziah separated them, the troops that had come to him out of Ephraim, to go home again. And their anger was greatly kindled against Judah, and they returned home in fierce anger.
Amaziah took courage and led forth his people, and went to the Valley of Salt, and smote of the children of Seir ten thousand.{e}
And the children of Judah carried away alive another ten thousand, and brought them to the top of the rock, and cast them down from the top of the rock, so that they all were broken in pieces.{f}

But the men of the troops whom Amaziah sent back, that they should not go with him to battle, fell upon the cities of Judah, from Samaria even to Beth-horon, and smote of them three thousand, and took much plunder.{g}
Now after Amaziah had come from the slaughter of the Edomites, he brought the gods of the children of Seir and set them up to be his gods, and bowed down before them and burned incense to them.

Therefore the anger of Yahweh was kindled against Amaziah, and he sent to him a prophet, who said to him, “Why have you sought after the gods of the people, which have not delivered their own people out of your hand?”

And as he talked with him, the king said to him, “Have we made you of the king’s counsel? Forbear; why should you be smitten?” Then the prophet forbore, and said, “I know that God has determined to destroy you, because you have done this and have not hearkened to my counsel.”{h}
Then Amaziah king of Judah took counsel and sent to Joash, the son of Jehoahaz, the son of Jehu, king of Israel, saying, “Come, let us look one another in the face.”{i}

And Joash king of Israel sent to Amaziah king of Judah, saying, “The thistle that was in Lebanon sent to the cedar that was in Lebanon, saying, ‘Give your daughter to my son as wife’; and there passed by a wild beast that was in Lebanon and trod down the thistle.{j}
You say, ‘See, I have smitten Edom,’ and your heart lifts you up to boast. Abide now at home; why should you meddle to your hurt, that you should fall, even you, and Judah with you?”{k}
But Amaziah would not hear; for it was of God, that he might deliver them into the hand of their enemies, because they had sought after the gods of Edom.
So Joash king of Israel went up, and he and Amaziah king of Judah looked one another in the face at Beth-shemesh, which belongs to Judah.{l}
And Judah was put to the worse before Israel, and they fled every man to his tent.

And Joash king of Israel took Amaziah king of Judah, the son of Joash, the son of Jehoahaz, at Beth-shemesh, and brought him to Jerusalem, and broke down the wall of Jerusalem from the gate of Ephraim to the corner gate, six hundred feet.{m}
And he took all the gold and silver, and all the vessels that were found in the house of God with Obed-edom, and the treasures of the king’s house, and the hostages, and returned to Samaria.{n}
Amaziah the son of Joash king of Judah lived after the death of Joash son of Jehoahaz king of Israel fifteen years.
Now the rest of the acts of Amaziah, first and last, behold, are they not written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel?
Now from the time that Amaziah turned away from following Yahweh, they made a conspiracy against him in Jerusalem; and he fled to Lachish, but they sent after him to Lachish and slew him there.{o}
And they brought him upon horses and buried him with his fathers in the city of Judah.{p}

notes.text: Amaziah, see 24:27; Jehoaddan, “Yahweh is delight.” Verses 1–4 parallel 2 Kings 14:1–6; verses 17–28 parallel 2 Kings 14:8–20.
Deuteronomy 24:16.
About 3.75 tons (3,400 kilograms) of silver. Hebrew “a hundred talents”; a talent was about 75 pounds or 34 kilograms. Verses 5–16 are not in Kings.
The Hebrew is difficult; some read “if you go thinking to be strong for the battle, God will cast you down.”
The Valley of Salt, probably south of the Dead Sea; compare 2 Kings 14:7, which says Amaziah also took Sela (“rock”).
“The rock,” Hebrew sela‘, perhaps the Edomite stronghold Sela (2 Kings 14:7).
Beth-horon, “house of the hollow.”
The play on words: “counsel” (Hebrew ya‘ats) runs through verses 16–17.
Joash king of Israel, also Jehoash; Jehoahaz, see 21:17; Jehu, see 19:2. The Ketiv has an extra word, “to you” or “go,” differing from the Qere.
Lebanon, “white,” for its snowy peaks.
Hebrew “You say, ‘Behold, you have smitten Edom’”; compare 2 Kings 14:10.
Beth-shemesh, “house of the sun.”
Hebrew “four hundred cubits,” about 600 feet or 180 meters; a cubit was about 18 inches or 45 centimeters.
Obed-edom, “servant of Edom”; a family of gatekeepers (1 Chronicles 26:15). This detail is not in Kings.
Lachish, meaning uncertain.
The Septuagint, and 2 Kings 14:20, read “in the city of David.”

verses.text: All the people of Judah took Uzziah, who was sixteen years old, and made him king in the place of his father Amaziah.{a}
He built Eloth and restored it to Judah, after the king slept with his fathers.{b}
Uzziah was sixteen years old when he began to reign, and he reigned fifty-two years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jecoliah of Jerusalem.{c}
He did that which was right in the eyes of Yahweh, according to all that his father Amaziah had done.
He set himself to seek God in the days of Zechariah, who had understanding in the vision of God; and as long as he sought Yahweh, God made him to prosper.{d}

He went forth and warred against the Philistines, and broke down the wall of Gath, the wall of Jabneh, and the wall of Ashdod; and he built cities in the country of Ashdod and among the Philistines.{e}
God helped him against the Philistines, and against the Arabians who dwelt in Gur-baal, and the Meunim.{f}
The Ammonites gave tribute to Uzziah, and his name spread abroad even to the entrance of Egypt, for he became exceedingly strong.
Moreover Uzziah built towers in Jerusalem at the corner gate, at the valley gate, and at the turning of the wall, and fortified them.

He built towers in the wilderness and hewed out many cisterns, for he had much cattle, both in the lowland and in the plain; and he had farmers and vinedressers in the mountains and in the fruitful fields, for he loved the soil.{g}

Moreover Uzziah had an army of fighting men that went out to war by bands, according to the number of their muster made by Jeiel the scribe and Maaseiah the officer, under the hand of Hananiah, one of the king’s captains.{h}
The whole number of the heads of fathers’ houses, mighty men of valor, was two thousand six hundred.
Under their hand was an army, three hundred and seven thousand five hundred, that made war with mighty power, to help the king against the enemy.
Uzziah prepared for them, for all the army, shields and spears and helmets and coats of mail and bows and stones for slinging.

And in Jerusalem he made engines, invented by skilful men, to be on the towers and on the battlements, to shoot arrows and great stones. And his name spread far abroad, for he was marvelously helped till he was strong.{i}

But when he was strong, his heart was lifted up, so that he did corruptly, and he trespassed against Yahweh his God; for he went into the temple of Yahweh to burn incense upon the altar of incense.{j}
And Azariah the priest went in after him, and with him eighty priests of Yahweh, who were valiant men.{k}

They withstood Uzziah the king and said to him, “It pertains not to you, Uzziah, to burn incense to Yahweh, but to the priests the sons of Aaron, who are consecrated to burn incense. Go out of the sanctuary, for you have trespassed; neither shall it be for your honor from Yahweh God.”{l}

Then Uzziah was wroth; and he had a censer in his hand to burn incense. And while he was wroth with the priests, a skin disease broke forth in his forehead before the priests in the house of Yahweh, beside the altar of incense.{m}

And Azariah the chief priest and all the priests looked upon him, and behold, he was diseased in his forehead, and they thrust him out quickly from there; yes, he himself also hasted to go out, because Yahweh had smitten him.

And Uzziah the king was diseased in his skin to the day of his death, and dwelt in a separate house, being so diseased; for he was cut off from the house of Yahweh. And Jotham his son was over the king’s house, judging the people of the land.{n}
Now the rest of the acts of Uzziah, first and last, Isaiah the prophet, the son of Amoz, wrote.{o}

So Uzziah slept with his fathers, and they buried him with his fathers in the field of burial which belonged to the kings; for they said, “He is diseased in his skin.” And Jotham his son reigned in his place.{p}

notes.text: Uzziah, “Yahweh is my strength”; called Azariah (“Yahweh has helped”) in 2 Kings 14:21; 15:1–7 and 1 Chronicles 3:12. Verses 1–4 parallel 2 Kings 14:21–22; 15:2–3.
Eloth, also Elath, “terebinths” or “palms,” at the head of the Gulf of Aqaba.
Jecoliah, “Yahweh is able.” The Ketiv and Qere differ slightly in spelling the name.
Zechariah, see 17:7. Hebrew “in the seeing of God”; the Septuagint and some Hebrew manuscripts read “in the fear of God,” which differs by vowels and one letter.
Gath, “winepress”; Jabneh, “he builds” (later Jamnia); Ashdod, meaning uncertain.
Gur-baal, perhaps “dwelling of Baal”; the Septuagint reads “on the rock.” Meunim, compare 20:1 note; the Septuagint reads “Minaeans.” The Ketiv and Qere differ in spelling “Arabians.”
Hebrew “the Shephelah,” the low hills west of Judah. Or “for he loved the land.”
Jeiel, see 20:14 (Ketiv Jeuel); Maaseiah, see 23:1; Hananiah, “Yahweh has been gracious.”
Perhaps catapults, or protective structures on the walls from which archers and slingers could shoot.
Verses 16–21 expand on 2 Kings 15:5, which does not give the cause of the disease.
Azariah, see 15:1.
Compare Numbers 16:40; 18:1–7.
Hebrew tsara‘at, a term for various skin diseases (not necessarily modern leprosy), which made a person ritually unclean (Leviticus 13). Older versions, “leprosy.”
Hebrew “a house of freedom,” perhaps a house of quarantine or release from duties; the Ketiv and Qere differ in spelling. Jotham, “Yahweh is perfect.”
Isaiah, “Yahweh is salvation”; Amoz, “strong.” Compare Isaiah 1:1; 6:1. This writing is not otherwise known.
Hebrew “He is diseased” (metsora‘). Compare 2 Kings 15:7.

verses.text: Jotham was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. His mother’s name was Jerushah the daughter of Zadok.{a}
He did that which was right in the eyes of Yahweh, according to all that his father Uzziah had done; however, he did not enter into the temple of Yahweh. And the people still did corruptly.{b}
He built the upper gate of the house of Yahweh, and on the wall of Ophel he built much.{c}
Moreover he built cities in the hill country of Judah, and in the forests he built fortresses and towers.

He fought also with the king of the children of Ammon and prevailed against them. And the children of Ammon gave him the same year about three and three-quarter tons of silver, and sixty thousand bushels of wheat, and sixty thousand of barley. So much did the children of Ammon pay him, both the second year and the third.{d}
So Jotham became mighty, because he ordered his ways before Yahweh his God.
Now the rest of the acts of Jotham, and all his wars and his ways, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Israel and Judah.
He was twenty-five years old when he began to reign, and reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem.
And Jotham slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city of David; and Ahaz his son reigned in his place.{e}

notes.text: Jerushah, “possessed”; Zadok, “righteous.” Chapter 27 parallels 2 Kings 15:32–38.
That is, he did not presume to burn incense as Uzziah had (26:16).
Ophel, “swelling” or “hill,” the fortified ridge south of the temple.

About 3.75 tons (3,400 kilograms) of silver, and about 60,000 bushels (2,200,000 liters) each of wheat and barley. Hebrew “a hundred talents … ten thousand cors”; a cor was about 6 bushels or 220 liters.
Ahaz, “he has grasped.”

verses.text: Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned sixteen years in Jerusalem. And he did not that which was right in the eyes of Yahweh, like David his father,{a}
but he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, and made also molten images for the Baals.
Moreover he burned incense in the valley of the son of Hinnom, and burned his children in the fire, according to the abominations of the nations whom Yahweh cast out before the children of Israel.{b}
He sacrificed also and burned incense in the high places, and on the hills, and under every green tree.

Therefore Yahweh his God delivered him into the hand of the king of Aram; and they smote him and carried away of his a great multitude of captives and brought them to Damascus. And he was also delivered into the hand of the king of Israel, who smote him with a great slaughter.{c}
For Pekah the son of Remaliah slew in Judah a hundred and twenty thousand in one day, all valiant men, because they had forsaken Yahweh, the God of their fathers.{d}
And Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim, slew Maaseiah the king’s son, and Azrikam the ruler of the house, and Elkanah who was next to the king.{e}
The children of Israel carried away captive of their brothers two hundred thousand women, sons, and daughters, and took also much plunder from them, and brought the plunder to Samaria.

But a prophet of Yahweh was there, whose name was Oded; and he went out to meet the army that came to Samaria, and said to them, “Behold, because Yahweh, the God of your fathers, was wroth with Judah, he has delivered them into your hand, and you have slain them in a rage that has reached up to heaven.{f}

And now you purpose to keep under the children of Judah and Jerusalem for bondmen and bondwomen to yourselves. But are there not with you, even with you, trespasses of your own against Yahweh your God?
Now hear me therefore, and send back the captives whom you have taken captive of your brothers; for the fierce wrath of Yahweh is upon you.”

Then certain of the heads of the children of Ephraim, Azariah the son of Johanan, Berechiah the son of Meshillemoth, Jehizkiah the son of Shallum, and Amasa the son of Hadlai, stood up against those who came from the war,{g}

and said to them, “You shall not bring in the captives here; for you purpose that which will bring upon us a trespass against Yahweh, to add to our sins and to our trespass; for our trespass is great, and there is fierce wrath against Israel.”
So the armed men left the captives and the plunder before the princes and all the assembly.

And the men who have been expressed by name rose up and took the captives, and with the plunder clothed all who were naked among them, and arrayed them, and shod them, and gave them to eat and to drink, and anointed them, and carried all the feeble of them upon donkeys, and brought them to Jericho, the city of palm trees, to their brothers. Then they returned to Samaria.{h}
At that time King Ahaz sent to the kings of Assyria to help him.{i}
For again the Edomites had come and smitten Judah and carried away captives.

The Philistines also had invaded the cities of the lowland and of the Negev of Judah, and had taken Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, Gederoth, and Soco and the towns of it, Timnah and the towns of it, and Gimzo and the towns of it; and they settled there.{j}
For Yahweh brought Judah low because of Ahaz king of Israel; for he had dealt wantonly in Judah and trespassed sorely against Yahweh.{k}
And Tilgath-pilneser king of Assyria came to him and distressed him, but did not strengthen him.{l}
For Ahaz took away a portion out of the house of Yahweh, and out of the house of the king and of the princes, and gave it to the king of Assyria; but it did not help him.{m}
And in the time of his distress he trespassed yet more against Yahweh, this same King Ahaz.

For he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus, which smote him; and he said, “Because the gods of the kings of Aram helped them, so will I sacrifice to them, that they may help me.” But they were the ruin of him and of all Israel.{n}

And Ahaz gathered together the vessels of the house of God, and cut in pieces the vessels of the house of God, and shut up the doors of the house of Yahweh; and he made himself altars in every corner of Jerusalem.{o}
And in every city of Judah he made high places to burn incense to other gods, and provoked to anger Yahweh, the God of his fathers.
Now the rest of his acts and all his ways, first and last, behold, they are written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel.
Ahaz slept with his fathers, and they buried him in the city, even in Jerusalem, because they brought him not into the sepulchres of the kings of Israel; and Hezekiah his son reigned in his place.{p}

notes.text: Ahaz, see 27:9. Verses 1–4 parallel 2 Kings 16:1–4. On his age and his son Hezekiah’s age (29:1), see 2 Kings 16:2 and 18:2; the figures are notoriously difficult to harmonize.
Hinnom, meaning uncertain; the valley south of Jerusalem (later Gehenna). Hebrew “burned his sons”; 2 Kings 16:3 reads “made his son pass through the fire.”
Compare 2 Kings 16:5–6 and Isaiah 7:1–9, which describe the joint Aramean–Israelite attack (the Syro-Ephraimite war) without reporting a defeat in battle.
Pekah, “opening (of the eyes)”; Remaliah, perhaps “Yahweh has adorned.” Verses 6–15 are not in Kings; on the large numbers, see 13:3 note.
Zichri, see 17:16; Maaseiah, see 23:1; Azrikam, “my help has arisen”; Elkanah, “God has created” or “acquired.”
Oded, see 15:1.

Azariah, see 15:1; Johanan, “Yahweh is gracious”; Berechiah, “Yahweh blesses”; Meshillemoth, “recompense”; Jehizkiah, “Yahweh strengthens” (a form of Hezekiah); Shallum, “recompense”; Amasa, “burden”; Hadlai, “resting.”
Jericho, perhaps “moon city” or “fragrant.” Compare Luke 10:30–37.
Hebrew “kings”; the Septuagint reads “king.” Compare 2 Kings 16:7, which names Tiglath-pileser.
Negev, “south” or “dry land.” Aijalon, “place of deer”; Gederoth, “walls” or “sheepfolds”; Soco, “thorny”; Timnah, “portion”; Gimzo, perhaps “place of sycamores.”
“King of Israel” here means king of Judah; compare 21:2 note. The Septuagint reads “king of Judah.”

Tilgath-pilneser, the Chronicler’s spelling of Tiglath-pileser III of Assyria (reigned about 745–727 BC); Hebrew tukulti-apil-esharra, “my trust is the son of Esharra.” Second Kings 16:9 says he did help Ahaz by taking Damascus; Chronicles stresses that the help brought Judah no lasting good.
Compare 2 Kings 16:8, 17–18.
Second Kings 16:10–16 says Ahaz copied an altar he saw in Damascus.
Second Kings 16:17–18 describes his removal of temple fixtures; the closing of the temple doors is reported only here (compare 29:3, 7).
Second Kings 16:20 says Ahaz was buried with his fathers in the city of David. Hezekiah, “Yahweh strengthens.”
